subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.

speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, April 15, the debate on the motion of Hon. J. A. Robb (Minister of Finance), that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the House to go into committee of Ways and Means.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before dealing with the subject matter of my address I want to compliment the Minister of Finance upon the presentation of his budget. It was concise, well put together and expressed in clear, terse language. I like the human touch which he gave in the concluding paragraph of his businesslike address, a touch that we sometimes lack in this House, and I compliment him on his very able presentation of a difficult subject. With the subject matter I shall try to deal as concisely as I possibly can.
I do not pretend to be a financial critic at all, Mr. Speaker, and what remarks I have to make in connection with the financial statement will be very largely a repetition of what the Minister of Finance has already told us in his budget statement. However, just to make it plain to myself at all events, I am going to run over some of the figures that he gave us at the commencement of his address.
He told us that the total estimated revenues for the year ended March 31, 1926, amounted to $376,800,000; that the estimated expenditures chargeable to consolidated fund amounted to $321,800,000, leaving a surplus of revenue over ordinary expenditure of $55,000,000.
Capital expenditure for public works amounted to $4,930,000; for railways and canals, $12,005,000, of which the larger amount, he explained, was for the Welland canal. The total net capital expenditure for the year amounted to $16,935,000. Other expenditures, such as the adjustment of war claims and the refunding of maturing war loans, amounted to $4,155,000, making a total of $21,090,000. Deducting this amount from $55,000,000 leaves a surplus of $33,910,000.
The total expenditure for all government services was $342,890,000, and the estimated revenue receipts for the year, $376,800,000 leaving a surplus of $33,910,000, as I have already said.
Then there have been special receipts and expenditures not included in the year's
fMr. Mcighen.]
business, one of which was the loan of $10,000,000 to the Canadian National Railway. There were, other special expenditures, bringing the total excess of special expenditures over special revenues to $11,557,000. This deducted from the $33,910,000 leaves a surplus of $22,353,000, which amount can be deducted from the national debt.
The national debt for 1925 amounted to $2,417,437,685.59 After deducting $22,353,000 from this amount, we have the total national debt at $2,395,084,685.59. I have no criticism to offer, Mr. Speaker, in connection with these figures. We are glad to know that there has been some slight reduction in the national debt, and that there is a surplus of $22,000,000 odd in the year's budget.
Now in regard to the estimates for the coming year, the amount named in the main estimates is $345,771,351. To this must be added other expenses and something for supplementary estimates, bringing the total for these additional expenses up to about $36,000,000, making the total estimated expenditure for the year $381,871,351. Looking over that amount it seems to me there is not going to be much less spent this year than last, and I think the minister has been quite optimistic in making up his budget when he thinks we are likely to have the amount of revenue he estimates for the year. If things go well and the country prospers during the next year, and we have a good crop, perhaps we may have a balanced budget, but if it should be otherwise, I am afraid it is just possible we may have a deficit instead of a surplus next year; but I am not going to pour cold water on the minister's hopes, and trust that we shall have a prosperous year;
There has been a wonderful revival of trade during the past year. Our exports increased over those of last year by the sum of $249,000,000. Our imports increased by $130,000,000 and our exports exceeded our imports by the sum of $402,695,000, I am inclined to believe, Mr. Speaker, that this large increase in our exports over our imports is largely due to the magnificent crop we had last year in the Dominion of Canada, more especially in the western provinces. Of this increased trade, 90 per cent is accounted for by empire trade. This, I am inclined to believe, would be made up very largely of our exports of agricultural and other natural products that we exported to Great Britain and other countries during the past year.
One of the encouraging features of our export trade is the large growth that has taken place in our export of cattle. For the year 1923 we exported cattle to the number

The Budget-Mr. Forke
of 25,758, valued at $2,809,796, and three years later, in 1926, we exported cattle to the number of 106,200, valued at $11,283,007, or almost five times the value of our exports three years previous, in 1923. This is very 'encouraging, and emphasizes the necessity of adequate provision being made in regard to the shipment of our cattle across the Atlantic ocean, and that freight rates be brought down to a proper point so that this trade may be increased.
Reviewing the cattle trade for a moment, during the years from 1901 to 1911, those wonderful growing years for Canada, when immigration was pouring into the country and we were building railroads and spending vast sums of money, we had a good trade in cattle, and the demand was domestic. These immigrants were pouring in, and hundreds of thousands of men were employed as railroad labourers, and they consumed nearly all the meat that was raised in the Dominion of Canada at that time. Consequently we had a good market then for our cattle. But then there came a flattening out about the year 1913, when things became very dull in the cattle trade. The war broke out in 1914, and we know what happened then. Prices rose very rapidly, and a ready market was found at high prices for all the cattle that we could raise. During the war the United States was glad to buy our cattle at high prices. But when the war was over, what happened? Our friends to the south again put up the fence. We had let our export trade go to pieces, and had no arrangements made for shipping cattle to Great Britain, and consequently the whole cattle trade fell very flat, and as a great many people are aware, a good many people were ruined. They were really bad times so far as the cattle trade was concerned. Since then we have tried to rearrange our cattle export trade to Great Britain, and as I have already pointed out we have made a considerable advancement in the three years from 1923 to 1926, almost $12,000,000 being received for the cattle we exported to Great Britain in the year 1923. This, Mr. Speaker, I think should be a reason why the government should be alive to the fact that it is necessary to see that proper bottoms and adequate accommodation are provided for the export of our cattle, and that freight rates on the Atlantic be reduced to the lowest possible point. It was rather unfortunate that the attempt that was made last year to make some advance in this direction did not succeed, but I hope the government will not be disheartened and that something will be done to see that this trade is properly taken care of.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: May I ask hon. members not to indulge in conversation. I cannot hear the speaker.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I want to say a few words in regard to our railway finances. The annual statement of the Canadian National Railways for the past year shows that the surplus of net earnings amounted to $33,000,000. This is very satisfactory indeed. The report goes on to say that the annual interest charges for the past year amounted to $71,-
800,000.	In the hands of the public there are interest bearing bonds and other securities amounting to $40,400,000, leaving a balance of $31,400,000 that is a liability to the government for interest and so on. Now if we take the $40,400,000 of interest that is due the public and deduct the $33,000,000 surplus of net revenue we find there is a deficit of $7,400,000. I am sure that when the public learns the fact that the deficit on the Canadian National Railway amounts to only $7,400,000 there will be a sigh of relief throughout the country. The statement goes on to say that during the year just closed the financial assistance to the railways by the government amounted to $10,000,000. There were no government guarantees and no floating indebtedness has been incurred. An unspent balance from 1925 of $2,700,000 has been utilized. The advance of $10,000,000 has been charged to the net debt of the Dominion, the railway loans being treated as non-active assets. I am inclined to believe they will be non-active for a very long time indeed. However, that is by the way. The loan of $10,000,000 covers the loss of $7,400,000 already referred to, leaving a balance of $2,600,000 for capital purposes. The total loans and payments made by the government to the railways now amount to $601,000,000. This includes interest and capital cost of the government railways. The financial position of the railways has improved immensely during the last few years, and no patriotic Canadian can read the statement without feeling proud of the achievements of the management of the Canadian National railways. A splendid service has been given the country, and year by year the system has been advancing until we are almost within measurable distance of the time when there will be a balanced budget, and perhaps in the not very far distant future these railways will be an asset to this Dominion instead of a liability.
I do not like to pass from a consideration of the railway situation without saying a word in regard to the Canadian Pacific Railway. Every patriotic Canadian wishes to see the Canadian National Railways flourish and become a profitable asset. At the same time

The Budget-Mr. Forke
he also wishes success to the Canadiaa Pacific Railway. There cannot be any other desire than that the Canadian Pacific should go on and prosper. It has done great things for Canada although, of course, many people think the country has done a great deal for the Canadian Pacific. Undoubtedly the interests of Canada and the Canadian Pacific are interwoven and when one flourishes the other must flourish also. Of course, we want our freight rates to be as low as they possibly can be. At the same time we can still carry on the battle and hold our end up. Our desire is that both the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific should flourish and prosper.
This leads me to say a few words in regard to income tax reduction, and I am going to read an extract from the Manitoba Free Press in regard to that subject which will give hon. members an idea of what the opinion in Manitoba at least is with regard to income tax reduction. The Manitoba Free Press says:
The cuts in taxation are all economically sound and politically judicious.
I hope my hon. friends to the right will notice the statement that what has been done is politically judicious anyway. The editorial goes on to say:
The rate of taxation upon automobiles was a scandal; once it was directly attacked as it was both last year and this session by Progressives and Liberal members, it became evident that it could not stand; but there was still the doubt whether the government would have the courage to deal with the question directly. To have passed the difficulty to the tariff board, which the government was beseeched to do would have been a political blunder of the first order. The tariff on automobiles is still substantial-27J per cent on cars costing over $1,200 and 20 per cent on cars below that figure. These rates, with a drawback of 25 per cent on raw material will still leave the automobile manufacturers in a strongly protected position, while the cuts will mean a substantial reduction in the price of cans. Those artless souls who think there is no connection between duties and prices are herewith advised to keep an eye for the next few weeks on the price of motors.
Mr. Speaker, to that last sentence I direct the attention of the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River who argued in this House a few days ago that the higher the protection was, the lower the price on the article would be. So I want that hon. member just to keep his eye on the price of cars for the next few weeks and see if it works out exactly in the way he imagines.

speechtext:
I will if I have time. Perhaps the hon. member will come round and instruct me.
I want to say a few words in regard to the payment of the income tax. I notice that the cuts in income tax were received with a great deal of jubilation by the great mass of people in the Dominion of Canada. I notice also that in some of the eastern papers the statement is made that since time has been afforded to study the question a reaction has taken place. I do not know why there should be any such reaction because it seems to me it was perfectly evident on the face of it what the reductions actually accomplished. I think the cuts in income tax are something we can all indorse. I am very much in favour of reducing the tax on small incomes, that is to say on small salaries up to $4,000. I think that anyone who knows anything about the living conditions in cities, where a man has a family to educate and bring up on a small salary, will realize he cannot afford to pay income tax on a salary much less than $4,000. That feature of the budget I am well inclined to endorse. At the same time I am a believer in the income tax. A vigorous campaign has been carried on, I know it has been carried on in the lobbies of the House, against the income tax as a tax at all, but I am a believer in direct taxation.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: As long as they do not tax you, I guess?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I pay my share of taxations anyway, at least I pay all that I am asked to pay. I have seen it stated that pain is a beneficent thing in the human body. It is a warning held out that something is wrong with the human system. We have sometimes been told that indirect taxation is a sort of painless extraction. It may be the same in the case of the body politic; there may be a painless extraction of taxes that may in the end prove fatal. I am inclined to think that the more we know of the taxes we are paying the better it will be from an individual and national point of view.
I was glad to hear the announcement of the Minister of Finance that there will be an estimated reduction of $25,000,000 in taxation.

The Budget-Mr. Forke
I think every one of us is anxious to see a reduction in taxation. Perhaps I might deal with that at the present time, although I intended to do so later. We continually hear it said that business cannot be carried on with the amount of taxes being collected at the present time. I wonder how we are going to get out of paying high taxes for a number of years. I know that we want economy in government. Every party when in opposition talks about economy, and every opposition generally blames the government for being extravagant, but we have found from experience that all governments are about the same, so far as extravagance goes, and I am inclined to believe that any reduction in the expense of carrying on the government is not going to amount to much. What are the conditions in Canada? We are reminded that taxes are now coming down in the United States and it is asserted that Canada must reduce taxation to the same level. But the comparison between conditions in Canada and the United States is not fair or just. Canada went into the Great war, and made great sacrifices which never can be made up. As a result of the financial sacrifices entailed by the great struggle we have a war debt. We have also a large debt on account of the Canadian National Railways which must be taken care of no matter who is to blame for the building of the railways. The United States before going into the war made vast sums of money out of it, and instead of the war placing them in a difficult financial position, they passed from being a debtor nation to a large creditor nation. The conditions in Canada and in the United States are not parallel, and I claim that Canadians who grumble and complain because they cannot get their taxes down to the same level as in the United States are not patriotic.
The incidence of taxation is perhaps just as important as the amount of taxes that a man may pay, and the question as to who pays the taxes is perhaps a more difficult question than a great many people believe. It is not always the men who are complaining the most who pay the taxes, and it is very important sometimes just to find out who is paying the taxes. We find business men complaining about the taxes. Manufacturers cannot carry ^ on, retailers and wholesalers cannot do business because they are paying too high taxes. How does a man conduct his business? What is the first thing he does? He finds out what his overhead will be, and what it costs him to produce a certain article, and his overhead is part of his expenses. If he cannot pay the taxes and carry on business he must go
out of business. My hon. friend to my right asks who is going to pay the taxes, and if I am paying my share of them. I raise cattle and I raise wheat, and most of my products are sold in the markets of Great Britain and the world, and when I pay my taxes will hon. gentlemen tell me of any method by which I can add my taxes on to the price of the article which I have to sell. I want hon. members to think over it for a minute. Do you know any way by which a farmer who raises products which have to be sold in the markets of the world can add the amount of his taxes to the price of the article he has to sell? So that I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the farmer or the agriculturist is just as much interested in the question of taxation as any man in business who is paying a large tax bill.
I have a few words to say in relation to the reduction that has been made in the taxation on automobiles. As has been stated in an article from a newspaper which I have read to the House, the general tariff is now reduced to 27i per cent and 20 per cent, and we find a tremendous wail going up from Canadian motor manufacturers over the reduction in taxation. I have great sympathy with our Canadian manufacturers, I want to see them prosper and do well in business, but, Mr. Speaker, if a business cannot be carried on with 27i and 20 per cent protection, it seems to me there is something wrong with that business. If we have more protection than that I claim the people of the Dominion are paying too much for their whistle and the Dominion as a whole would perhaps be in as good a position without the industry. I am not saying for one moment that we are going to do without them, but I repeat that if they cannot carry on with 27i per cent protection there is something wrong with the industry.	.
I picked up a newspaper the morning after the budget had been delivered in the House by the Finance Minister, and I saw what probably all hon. members of the House saw. We read the statement that a certain institution had closed its doors; it was a gloomy day, 3,000 people marched out in the morning to go to work, and found the door shut in their face. The whole situation was dramatic. The manager stated that they had to close their doors because they wished to look over the situation. Perhaps that was the reason, but I have seen a farmer's crop destroyed in ten minutes by a hail storm, his whole season's work gone, and the next morning he pulled out his team and plough and started to prepare for the next year.
The Budget-Mr. Forke

speechtext:
I clipped this out of a
Toronto newspaper and it ought to be correct There is in the budget some slight indication that the government has remembered the man on the street and the people at large. I have no intention of changing my position in regard to protection and I should like to say a few words regarding what is called adequate protection. The extract that I have just read is an advertisement from an industry that sometimes complains from lack of protection. A few minutes ago I said that it was not fair to be always comparing Canada with the United States. We are continually told that the United States have been prosperous because of their high protective walls, but conditions in the two countries are not parallel. In Canada we have a temperate climate from the Atlantic to the Pacific whereas in the United States they have every variety of climate. They can if they so wish be a self-contained country and produce everything that human beings require. In Canada under modern civilization we must, from the very necessity of thing?, import a large quantity of the products we consume daily, and that is one of the aspects of the case which we must take into consideration when we are comparing United States with Canada.
The United States, however, is not so self-contained as one would imagine and I will read just a Short extract showing what that country is importing even with its high tariff. In 1925, the United States imported $1,818,000,000 worth of agricultural products, $1,000,000,000 worth of which were in direct competition with their own products. I should be glad to have any member tell me why the United States would import $1,000,000,000 worth of agricultural products that they could raise within their boundaries. I can tell hon. members the reason. It was because other countries could raise them so much cheaper than the United States could.
This is a short extract from a communication by Tom King from Washington. Mr. King said:
By a curious twist of circumstances, the price often goes down when the tariff goes up.
A funny thing.
This temporarily disconcerts the protectionist, though later on he will seriously argue that raising the tariff permanently lowers the price.
We know that. That argument has been made in this House.
It so happens that ever since President Coolidge announced that the future tariff on butter should be twelve cents instead of eight cents a -pound, butter has been higher in Montreal than it has been in New York. Indeed, the American butter market is quite demoralized, and Canadian cream has gone up..

The Budget-Mr. Forke
That shows that even with protection trade will follow the path of least resistance.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

I do not see what is wrong
with that. A proposition has been made by members on both sides to compensate western farmers for protection. I think the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) made the proposition at one time-if I am wrong, he will correct me-that something might be done in the way of bonusing the western farmer by means of lower freight rates to compensate them for the high prices he is charged on account of protection. I know if he did not make that proposition, the hon. member who sat in the last parliament for the constituency of St. Lawrence-St. George proposed in the House that freight rates should be lowered for the western farmer to compensate him for the extra price he had to pay under protection. That was economically unsound and impracticable and I would not have anything to do with it. But I value a statement of that kind from the leader of the opposition and from Mr. Marler who sat in this House as a Liberal as showing that they admitted that the western farmer was handicapped and paid a tax because there were high protective duties in the country.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I am going to pay the leader of the opposition a compliment. He stated my understanding of the matter in better language than I could. I do not think the average farmer in the Dominion has much to fear as regards being swamped by agricultural products coming in from the United States. I have a friend back in Manitoba whose family have been milking twenty-five cows all winter. They work hard; the women have to do their share, and this idea of protecting an industry has something very enticing about it. My friend does not pay very much attention to politics or economics, and I know if someone went to him and told him that if the government would put a duty of three cents on butter he would get a much better price for his cream, he would immediately say: Why do they not do so? That is exactly how the farmer is Jed astray in regard to the question of protecting his products. I am sure the dairy farmer of the Dominion of Canada has very little to fear from outside competition. No butter that crosses the
Pacific from Australia will ever come into competition with fresh dairy-made butter in this country, and the only time that there will be any competition will be under normal conditions when we are suffering from a shortage of butter. I can remember when the oleomargarine debate took place in the House and terrible pictures were drawn of conditions in the cities because children would have to use oleomargarine instead of getting wholesome butter. When butter during the winter reaches such a high price that the poorer people in the cities are unable to pay it, the farmers of the Dominion will not want any protection that will compel these people to use oleomargarine or any other substitute.
This idea of protection is very enticing. I have been trying anxiously during the present session of parliament to find out just what the position of the leader of the opposition and some of the members who sit on that side is in regard to protection. I had an idea during election time that they were in favour of very high protection-brick for brick.

speechtext: No, no.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I am going to read a few extracts that I have in my hand and after I have read them perhaps we shall have a better idea of what protection means to my hon. friends to my right. I will read a few extracts from speeches delivered by the leader of the opposition during the election campaign. We know that the only thing for us to do is to get up and stand on our feet, adopt the methods that have brought the United States where they are to-day.

Well, they ought to be for
I have been a workingman all my life and know something about work. Let me quote a few words by Sir John Willison in regard to the future of our manufacturing industries, and I do not think any of my hon. friends will question such an authority. Not very long ago he said that:
Manufacturing industry in Canada would not be successful unless it was underpinned and supported by the energy, the ability and the enterprise of the Canadian people producing excellent goods at a reasonable price.
Could you get any better doctrine than that? If our manufacturers would) keep that before their eyes and not think so much about protection, they would not be in the difficult position that they sometimes find themselves in. We talk about sectionalism and selfishness. Well, we are all human and all of us are bound to be a little selfish and a little sectional, no one can be in this House for four or five sessions without realizing that generally we are representing the problems of our own particular constituencies. That is quite natural. We cannot put forward the requirements of our own districts without to a certain extent being either sectional or selfish. At the same time let us take a broad view of the whole situation. I know the Progressives are being continually condemned by the press-and I want to speak quite moderately in this connection-by the eastern papers especially, as working only for our own interests. Well, the Progressives, like the members of every other party in the House, are looking after their sections of the Dominion, and it is quite possible to look after the best interests of your own locality and yet preserve a broad view and work for the interests of the whole Dominion. Last week Mr. Calder spoke in the Chateau Laurier on the subject of "A House Divided." I made a humble attempt the other day at Toronto to speak upon "Canadian Unity." I am prepared in this House and in the country, Mr. Speaker, to stand up for Canadian unity, for a united Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and I submit that those who are continually holding up certain members of the House as being selfish and sectional in their views are not doing what will tend to unity of sentiment and action throughout this country; on the contrary they are trying to split the east from the west. If I can do anything in public life I hope it will be to draw those two great sections of the Dominion closer together.
	*
During this session we have heard a great deal about Maritime rights. I can assure the House that when we came here at the beginning of the session no member of the Progressive party from western Canada was indifferent to the grievances of our Maritime friends, and every one of us was and is anxious to do everything possible to help them. Entertaining these sentiments, I was all the more sorry to hear members from the Maritimes now and then finding fault with what they called the sectional and narrow point of view that the western members were taking. I hope the people of the Maritimes will solve their difficulties in a very short time and that in the years to come that important and historic portion of Canada will be very prosperous.
What has made the present budget possible? What has enabled the Minister of Finance to tell us that he is able to reduce our taxation by $25,000,000? Do not all members believe that the tremendous crop we had last year is the main reason for the prosperity which we are now enjoying? We are continually attempting to develop the country from the wrong end. Our friends living in the cities and close to manufacturing concerns naturally imagine that we can be made prosperous by enlarging our industrial plants.

We have had hard times in years gone by in Canada, but I am inclined to think that we have reached the top of the hill and that from now on the going will be easier. The west has produced a vast amount of wealth during the past year, amounting in the aggregate to a very large sum, over $900,000,000, as was stated very clearly by the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett), in the House a few days ago. That is a vast amount of money, but still there are people out there who have difficulty in making ends meet, and it is not very nice for them to read about the growing prosperity of our country. But I believe, Mr. Speaker, that times are going to improve, and that we are going to have better conditions, with better prices. I want to assure hon. members and those who read my speech, both manufacturers, business men and others, that there is no antagonism in western Canada towards industry as such, that any action we are taking is not a matter of antagonism, but simply a matter of self-preservation. We have difficulties in Canada, we have troubles, but notwithstanding hard times, I believe there is more individual happiness in this Dominion at the present time than there is in any other country in the world. We are still in the year 1926 trying to adjust ourselves to new world conditions, but I believe that we are going to be successful, and that we are going to have better times.
There are two words, Mr. Speaker, which I have heard mentioned in this House. I would not mention them to-day except that I want to make my opinions and my ideas plain. Those words are secession and annexation. Those are two words I do not want to have anything to do with, and I mention them now only to make my opinions plain to this House. We sometimes hear that this country is being invaded by a process of what we might call peaceful penetration, and I believe there is some truth in that statement. Last year Canada paid $4,500,000 for American newspapers and American magazines. I am not going to say anything against American publications other than this, that we have a few high-class magazines in the United States coming into Canada which I should be very sorry to see stopped from coming into this country, but the point I want to make is this: What is the influence of this tremendous amount of American literature that is being read by our Canadian people at the present time? I do not believe they are aware themselves just how much they are being influenced by what they read, but this is a fact I am calling to your attention.

It is not a matter I would play politics with at all for one moment, and if I thought a duty on American magazines would be the right thing, I would tell the leader of the opposition so right away. But I do not know. There are two sides to the question, and it is a very difficult one to settle. I only mention this to show what is taking place.
There are some people who say that Canada would prosper much more quickly if we were part of the United States. I do not believe that for one moment. I read somewhere lately, I forget just where, that the state of Washington is no more prosperous than the province of British Columbia; it is not as prosperous or as progressive. Are the two Dakotas and Montana any more prosperous than the prairie provinces? They are not at the present time. The farmers and the rural population in those three states are not as prosperous as the people in our three prairie provinces, and when you come down to Ontario, this province is just as prosperous as the state of Wisconsin or some other states to the south. Would my good friends from the province of Quebec change places with any of the New England states? No, I am sure they would rather be Quebec.

Then why are our
people leaving for the United States?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
We find that the great
wealth of the United States is being centered in certain places to the south, and that the northern tier of states is 'being left very much out in the cold. We are a still more northerly tier, and I am inclined to believe that were we joined with the United States, we would be worse off still. I say to my fellow Canadians: Stay with Canada. Canada is our country. I have mentioned in this House before that I am not a native-born Canadian, but Canada is my home, and every interest I have is in Canada, and I expect great things of this country. Mr. Speaker, Canada has a destiny of its own to fulfil. It can fill a place in the world's history. It can give something to increase the happiness and welfare of humanity if we

will only follow the course we ought to pursue. I want to see Canadian national unity. I do not know just how to bring it about. On the one hand, we have the east wanting high protection, and on the other, the west wanting low tariff. We must find some com-imon ground of agreement, some stopping place. However, in the meantime I hope all of us will pursue our daily vocations with industry and intelligence, trying to work out our own destiny and that of our nation.
I want to see Canada still retain her place within the British Empire. This is not the place to begin a discussion of Canada's status and her place among the nations of the world, but I want to see Canada a free nation, taking her place among the galaxy of nations. I know a whole lot of difficulties surround this question. You cannot exactly state in words the position we occupy to-day, but I should like to see our country in the years to come still a part of the great British Empire. I believe that our safety in the future, and for a great many years to come, will lie in the fact that we belong to the British Empire. Therefore I hope that we will not forget this idea.
In closing I want to quote a few words that I came across the other day. I do not know who the author is but this is his description of our Dominion:
Canada a daughter of the empire, grown to be a potent factor; but equally strong in loyalty to the British commonwealth, clear visioned-sound in wind and limb, a great race in a great country, coveting nothing, shaping and working out for itseLf with high courage, energy and ability a great destiny.
As my last word I want to say that at this time, no matter in what quarter of the House we may sit, we will be Canadians, loyal to our country and believing in its future. Canada wants men with broad vision and with faith in themselves and in their country. Given these conditions, notwithstanding our political struggles and differences, I have no fear for the future of this great Dominion.

He did what has become quite a habit, and I suppose has been a habit with politicians for a long t:me, he put into my mouth words which I have never used. I took down the hon. gentleman's statement at the time it was made. He said that I had stated in this House that "the higher the tariff the lower the price." Well, of course, it is hardly necessary for me to say that I never made any such statement. What I did state here the other day, in a little dispute across the floor, was that the raising of the tariff does not necessarily mean an increase in the price. He went on to ask for a definition of what our tariff policy was. I will give him one definition of what the tariff policy of the Liberal Conservative party is and it is this: It is a tariff policy to build up Canada and not to build up the United States, or any other foreign country.
The hon. gentleman spent some time ridiculing the idea that any of these automobile industries will suffer because of the tariff which has been brought in, and he pointed out that they practically would not be injured at all. Well, I am going to read a statement made by the president of the United States General Motors, Mr. Sloan. He made a statement on the subject in New York the other day and this is what he said:
There has not been sufficient time ito analyse the effect of the Canadian tariff changes, but it is very evident that it means the transfer of Canadian plants to American factories, or, in other words, the elimination of a corresponding amount of Canadian labour. Due to the fact that production in Canada will be reduced it is only fair to assume that there wild be correspondingly increased profits for American manufacturers.
That is the attitude of a New Yorker, the president of the United States General Motors, a man who is not interested in Canadian work, except in taking Canadian work from Canadian people.
And may I add this: That at the present time, and I do not think the statement can be contradicted, the tariff on automobiles coming into Canada is lower than the tariff on automobiles going into any country in the world that manufactures automobiles, and I do not except even England in this statement. speechtext:
I hope that I shall always be a loyal enough Canadian to rejoice with the Canadian people when conditions in this country have improved for them. I wish to congratulate the Minister of Finance in being able to bring in a budget which shows an increase in revenue of something like $29,000,000. The Finance Minister also shows a better condition of the railways, as well as-and this I do not dispute-some taxation reductions with which I shall deal briefly as I pass on. In other words the Finance Minister points out that conditions are better in Canada today than they have been during the past four years. I do not dispute his conclusions in that respect, but also as a Canadian I make this statement, that after looking into the whole question as completely as I can, and laying aside also as completely as I can whatever partisanship I may feel, I am sure this better condition in Cianada to-day is, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Brandon, as a matter of fact due to the good fortune of the Canadian people and not to the good management of this government. The reason I say that is because the tariff policy, the unwise tariff policy of this government, has in the past four years unsettled the business affairs of Canada, injured the industries of the country, lessened the work and wages of the people, and increased the exodus of Canadians to the United States.
And by the extravagances of which they have been guilty they have increased the taxes, or failed to permit the decrease of taxes, which should have taken place. With

reference to the estimates which we have before us this year of the expenditures of the government, the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke), who is certainly not a friend of hon. members on this side of the House, pointed out that these estimates are a good deal higher than the estimates of last year. I was going to point out that last year's estimates were $351,000,000. This year's ordinary estimates are $345,000,000, or $6,000,000 less than last year, but the supplementary estimates have yet to be presented, and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) in his budget speech admitted that the supplementary estimates would increase the general estimates to such an extent as to make the year's estimates equal to the $351,000,000 in the estimates last year. But as was pointed out by the hon. member for Brandon, the old age pensions were not taken into account, the advances to the settlers act expenditure was not taken into account, nor was the expenditure for the Soldier Settlement Board. The Old Age Pension Act alone, if carried out by the people of this country in co-operation with the provinces, means another expenditure of $11,000,000 or $12,000,000 per annum, the land settlement act means another $1,000,000 and the relinquishment of the debts owing to the government under the Soldier Settlement Act many millions more. So that I submit, in agreement with the hon. member for Brandon, that this year's estimates are going to be very much higher than those of last year. In other words, this government goes on gaily spending the people's money, ignoring the fact that the burden of taxation presses very severely upon the shoulders of the people, and ignoring the opportunity to reduce that taxation.
Now, I submit, Mr. Speaker, that just as the best judge of a dinner is not the cook but the diner, so the best judge of this budget is not the Finance Minister who presented it, but the people of Canada, and after the budget is analyzed by this House and passes to the people of Canada, they will owe a great deal more of Christian forgiveness to the government than they will owe of gratitude.
Why did I make the statement that the improved conditions in Canada were due more to good fortune than to any good management on the part of the government? Because in the first place, so far as I can remember- I say it in all seriousness, and I am open to correction by speakers following me if I am wrong-I know of no act of this government in the four years it has been in power which improved or tended to improve conditions in Canada. I submit that a kind Providence ha3 seen that the Canadian people have not

The Budget-Mr. Manion
suffered all the ill effects of the unwise tariff policy and unwarranted extravagance of the late government, and I intend to give figures very briefly showing where Providence has been kind to Canada. That the improvement is due to Providence is shown by the fact that in 1925 our agricultural production was $265,000,000 greater than in 1924. In mineral production the amount was $15,000,000 greater-
I obtained these figures from the Department of Statistics-and in unmanufactured wood-these are exports; I could not get the production -a favourable balance of $5,000,000. There was an increased production in 1925 over that of 1924, to the extent of $285,000,000. That has been in no way the result of the efforts of the government; it has been the bounty of Providence. In other words, the government is not in any way responsible for that bounty to the people of Canada. The increase of $285,000,000-nearly $300,000,000- means that the people had a very much greater purchasing power than they had the year before; that the railways handled a very much greater traffic; and a consequent increase in government revenue. I admit that luck has been with this government; that Providence, by giving Canada these greater crops, has shown some favour to the present administration. But there is a Providence, they say, which looks after drunken men, and I presume the same Providence looks after governments who are drunken with the desire to hold power in spite of the wishes of the people.
Now I wish to deal very briefly with some of the alleged decreases in taxation dealt with by the Minister of Finance in his budget-though I shall leave the more thorough investigation of this matter to my good friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton) whom we are glad to see back in the House-in relation to postage rates, receipt tax, income tax and, in a few minor respects, the sales tax. In regard to the sales tax, it was under our regime three per cent, but this government raised it to six per cent. Two years ago fhey lowered it to five per cent, where it still stands. The sales tax is a distinct tax upon all the people of Canada. It would be very much better to remove that tax than to remove the tariff on automobiles. I may say further that if we are to judge of the probable reduction in the prices of automobiles as is indicated by the figures published by the Ford people, the removal of the five per cent sales tax would have a greater effect in cutting the price of automobiles than the action taken by the Minister of Finance. It would not endanger the employment of thousands of workmen in Canada and raise the 14011-167
possibility of tens of thousands more of the Canadian people being forced to go to the most highly protected country in the world, the United States, to earn a living.
The receipt tax was not a tax of the old government, but was put on by this government. I am glad it is off. But a much more important tax, .which should also be off, and which was increased by this government, is the cheque tax. It was two cents when the former government went out of power, and it was increased on cheques for larger amounts by this government. That is a more unjust tax than the receipt tax, because the man who puts the stamp on the cheque is the man who is paying the money, and the man who puts the stamp on the receipt is the man who is receiving the money. I submit both these taxes should be off, and if the government had done away with unnecessary extravagances it could have taken both off.
In regard to the income tax, I believe that while the reductions in some cases will be of assistance to the people of Canada, in other cases they will prove of no benefit ; in fact in many cases they are no reduction at all but an increase. Take the case of a widow whose husband created an income of $5,000 in dividends, which she inherits. She would not have paid any tax in the past, but will have to pay under the new scheme. A retired gentleman of 72 or 73 years of age, with whom I sat at a meal the other day, receives, with his pension from the business he followed, an income of $2,800. His wife had the good fortune to inherit $2,000 per annum, so that this old couple, who were accustomed to living reasonably well on $4,800, were paying last year an income tax of four per cent on $800, each of them having an exemption of $2,000. He paid an income tax of 4 per cent on $800 which would be $32. But this old couple, in the autumn of their lives, are now going to pay more. They are allowed $1,500 exemption, so that he will pay two per cent on $1,300 or $26 as against $32 the year before, while in addition to that his wife will now be paying two per cent on $500 or $10, a total of $36. What is the object of this? In studying the new income tax schedules I was interested to note the variations in amounts payable. While this old couple have to pay increased taxation, those who for example make $14,009 a year have had a reduction of some $474.50 in their income tax. I do not wish to be unfair or unkind, but one might ask oneself whether those material reductions that have been made on the $14,000 salary have anything to do with the fact that members of the government receive $14,000 a year.

The Budget-Mr. Manion

Is it fair that this old couple of seventy-two or seventy-three should have their taxes increased while those getting $14,000 a year get this marked decrease? I was thinking of a jocular statement made by Mr. Lloyd George at one time when he was speaking of another government and I felt I could in the same jocular way apply the statement to this government. His statement was:
The members of this government will go down with their drawn salaries in their hands.
The postage rate has been reduced from three cents to two cents and everybody will be glad of that reduction. But this reduction could have been made long ago if the government had not given those unnecessary political bribes which were used throughout the country; for instance, millions of dollars spent for harbours which was not required to be spent, millions of dollars spent for public works, inaccessible elevators and other things such as the Union Club in London.
But after going all down these different reductions as mentioned by the Minister of Finance, I find myself wondering where the ordinary workingman who does not earn $3,000 a year, and the ordinary small farmer who does not happen to have an automobile, benefits by any of these reductions. I can find nothing with the exception that once in a while when he sends a letter to somebody away from home he saves one cent on his postage stamp. Where is the relief for the workingman who earns less than $3,000 a year unless it be that he is relieved of his job in some of those factories that are being closed on account of this budget? A very large percentage, I think much more than ninety per cent of the workingmen of Canada, will not benefit by these reductions. In other words, I found myself wondering if this budget was one entirely for the betterment of the rich and the Well-to-do, because I discovered that the rich man by this budget gets his income tax reduced, his high-priced automobile at a lesser duty, and even his Angostura bitters cheaper for his cocktail. I presume the government is hoping that at election time he will drink his cocktails to their health.
There is little if anything, in this budget for the poor people. I think it was Abraham Lincoln who said: "God must love the poor because he made so many of them." If he was alive now, he could not say that about this government because they are making the poor poorer by taking away their jobs, and making the rich richer by taking away their income tax.

I do not wish to spend any more time on these taxes; I wish to touch what is to me and, I think, to the people of Canada, the most important item in the whole budget and that is the cut in the duty on automobiles. That is the axle around which this whole budget is going to revolve, when the people have forgotten the superficial reductions in taxation mentioned by the Minister of Finance, when, in fact, the resulting relief mentioned by him is found to be a delusion and a snare, and when they realize also that this is another very severe assault upon the national policy of protection which has been in force in Canada since 1878. Once again the issue is clear-cut and well defined; the issue has come before the people as to whether we shall have protection in this country or whether we shall go down towards free trade.
Before dealing with the reduction in the tariff on automobiles I wish to say that I have no brief in any way for the automobile industry. In my riding there are no plants manufacturing automobiles or automobile parts. As a doctor practising medicine when I am at home, I have occasionally to buy an automobile and therefore I would probably stand to gain a little if prices are reduced because of this reduction in the tariff. But at the same time, as a Canadian, I am willing, if necessary, to pay a little more for my automobile or for any other line of goods in order to build up this great country of ours. Neither am I arguing from the point of view that the majority who cannot afford to buy automobiles of any kind will gain; nothing by this reduction in the tariff on automobiles. An automobile being a luxury in many cases should, I think, be taxed more highly-I do not say in all cases. It is only right that luxuries should be taxed at a higher rate than necessaries of life and certain high-priced automobiles are luxuries. Neither do I point out the fact that in many cases people bring about less happiness to themselves by securing automobiles at the cost of a mortgage on their home or on their life insurance, at the cost of that thrift which we should all encourage as good citizens of Canada. Neither do I deny nor assert that this tariff cut is not bearable by the automobile industry of this country. Time alone will answer that question.
But I assert this, that in justice to the people, and to the automobile industry of Canada, the tariff board which was appointed just eight days before the delivery of the budget, should have been given an opportunity to look into this industry before these cuts in the tariff were made. If such had

The Budget-Mr. Manion
been the case and if the tariff board had reported that these automobile manufacturers were exploiting, were taking unfair profits from the people of Canada behind a tariff wall, then I say they should either bring down their prices or have their tariff removed to a certain extent to make them deal justly with the Canadian people. It is no part of the policy of the Conservative party to allow unfair prices to the people to be put into effect behind a tariff wall by manufacturers of automobiles or any other manufacturers. But there should have been an investigation, because we have had in Canada, I repeat, a policy of protection since 1878, and so fai las I know on every occasion when the people have been given an opportunity to vote on that question, they have voted to carry on a policy of protection.
There are three outstanding dates:	1878.
1911 and 1925. I mention 1925 because it is plain that on October 29, 1925, the 116 members on our side of the House were elected on a protective policy, and it is also plain that on the other side there are many members, probably forty, if not fifty or sixty, who are out-and-out protectionists, just as much as the protectionists who sit on this side of the House. For example, would anybody question the fact that the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) is an out-and-out protectionist, or that the hon. member for North Bruce (Mr. Malcolm), who is spoken of as being slated for the cabinet, is an out-and-out protectionist? Would anyone say that many hon. members from Quebec are anything but protectionists? The hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Denis) in this House not long ago in the debate on the Address said frankly and plainly that he believed in protection. Indeed, I am reminded by an hon. member that he said he was elected on that policy.
In other words, the election of October 29, no matter what else it did, certainly showed that the people of Canada, with the exception probably of those in the prairie provinces, believe in a policy of protection. It showed that this government is not in agreement with the people of Canada generally, and you may take it for granted as a political axiom that when a government differs from the people of a country, the people are right and the government is wrong.

speechtext:
The people defeated us

defeated this government and the government did not go out of power. That is the difference.
On what basis did this government make this reduction in the tariff on automobiles eight days after it had appointed a tariff board supposedly for the purpose of looking into industries such as this? They cast aside that tariff board like a sucked orange eight days after they appointed it and they cut down the tariff on automobiles. I will give the reasons of the Minister of Finance for cutting down the tariff on automobiles. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), at page 2450 of Hansard, made this statement:
There is a pronounced sentiment throughout Canada that the automobile industry enjoys more protection than is needed to maintain it on a reasonably profitable basis, and in deference to that Bentiment we propose a downward readjustment of automobile, motor truck and motor cycle duties.
"In deference to sentiment throughout Canada!" I wonder why it is that this government has become so suddenly deferential to the sentiment of the Canadian people. Hon. gentlemen opposite did not show any great desire to defer to the clearly indicated wish of the people of this country when on October 29 last, as a result of the general election held at that time, the Canadian electorate showed beyond any question that they no longer wanted this government in power. The government was defeated, whatever else the election may have revealed. But it is not that the Minister of Finance and the government, in making this reduction in the tariff, felt that there was a pronounced sentiment in the country in favour of it. The fact of the matter is that they believe there is a pronounced number of votes to be gained by this concession when the time comes. That explains why the tariff on automobiles has been reduced to the extent disclosed in the budget. The government does not care what irreparable injury is done to Canadian industry so long as it can remain in office. So far as our working population is concerned, every artisan may be driven out of Canada into the United States, provided the government can remain in power. Scientific knowledge and economic investigation, which should have been the duty of the tariff commission, are of course unnecessary to this government. What is necessary is the government's popularity: it is essential that hon. gentlemen opposite should obtain a sufficient number of votes to keep them in power. In short, our workingmen must be exiled in order to maintain the present administration in office.
We hear less about an exodus now than we heard in the past, and we read less of it in the
[DOT] 2G2S
The Budget-Mr. Manion

press at the present time. Tie exodus, everyone admits, is not so ina/kid to-day as it was formerly. I have in my hand, however, an extract from the Toronto Globe of a few days ago in which the statement appears that
53,000	Canadians left this country and went to the United States in the seven months ending January 31 last, or at the rate of nearly 100,000 per annum. In making this statement the Toronto Globe is quoting from the report of an investigating organization in the United States, and the statement is not denied. Now, if this budget does the harm which many people throughout Canada believe it will do, there will be more people going to the United States shortly than have left Canada in the past.
I can quite imagine that many of our workingmen in Canada must find themselves asking this question, "Why should we be made the sacrificial goats in order to keep this government in office?" In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the present Prime Minister of Canada through his tariff policy has been the greatest immigration agent the United States has ever had. What ri^ht has this government to make an unwarranted onslaught on the tariff policy which has been in force in this country since 1878, having been accepted and endorsed repeatedly from that time on? What right have hon. gentlemen to break the pledges which they have only recently given to this country, that no industry should be interfered with in the absence of a proper investigation? What right have they to disturb business conditions in Canada and to bring about such instability as we have witnessed during the past four years?-an instability by reason of which no industrial leader in Canada to-day dare invest his money in industry lest his own head be taken off and earned on a salver to the low tariff or free trade forces of the country who control the government.
So far as tariff matters are concerned, this government seems to live in a thick fog of confused ideas; it changes its economic mind so often that it is impossible for any sane man to follow it. The tariff history of the government would appear to me to be something for the government to forget and for everybody else in Canada to remember. But what other attitude could you expect from the government when you look around on its members and realize that there are three ministers from Saskatchewan, that free track province, for which let me say, I have every respect. There are from that province three ministers in prominent positions-the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), the Prime Minister himself (Mr. Mackenzie King),
[Mr. Manion.l
and the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning). And from the west we have also the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart, Edmonton), the author of that famous phrase about the death-knell of protection. When the Minister of Railways came into the House the newspapers declared that, like charity, he was expected to cover a multitude of sins for the government. Well, the Minister of Railways has taken a very frank stand on the tariff. There was passed in the legislative assembly of Saskatchewan, in the session of 1923, a resolution which practically proposes free trade for the Dominion of Canada. Perhaps I may be allowed to quote that part of the resolution bearing on this question. It proposed:
(1)	An immediate and substantial all round reduction of the customs tariff.
(2)	The reduction of the customs duty on goods imported from Great Britain to one-half of the rates charged under the general tariff, and that further gradual uniform reductions be made to the remaining tariff on British imports that will insure complete free trade between Great Britain and Canada.
(3)	That negotiations be entered into by the government of Canada with the government of the United States with a view of establishing a reciprocity agreement on lines similar to that of 1911.
(4)	The .placing upon the free list of all food stuffs, agricultural implements, farm and household machinery, vehicles, fertilizers, coal, lumber, cement, gasoline, illuminating fuel and lubricating oils, and all raw materials and machinery used in their manufacture.
The report concludes with the statement that, a debate arising the question was put and was agreed to unanimously.

but I wish to point this out: Just the other day the tariff on our butter going into the United States was raised to three times our tariff on United States butter coming into Canada; before that the tariff was just double. Let me put this to any of our good farming friends in this House, and they are not all to my left or sitting opposite; there are quite a lot of them behind me in this party. Suppose they drive in to town with a load of butter or potatoes or some other farm pro-
The Budget-Mr. Manion

duction and go into a store in Toronto, say. or Montreal, and tell the storekeeper that they have a load of potatoes for sale. Suppose the storekeeper says, "I will not have anything to do with your potatoes. Get out of my shop. I will not handle your goods at any price,"-and that is what the Americans are saying to the Canadian agriculturist at the present time-what would the Canadian farmer reply to the storekeeper? Would he say, "You won't buy my goods, but I would like to buy some of yours?" No, he has too much red blood in him to say that. He would say to the storekeeper, "You do not need to buy my goods, and I do not need to buy yours. I will treat you as you treat me." And that should be our attitude towards the United States. Why should we have a tariff of only four cents a pound on United States butter coming into Canada, when they have a tariff of twelve cents a pound against our butter? As a consequence of the fact that our tariffs on agricultural products are so low as compared with the United States tariffs on the same goods, we imported last year $150,000,000 worth of agricultural products which could have been produced on the farms of Canada. Do not misunderstand me; I am not speaking of tropical fruits, or cotton, but simply of products that could have been produced on the farms of Canada, and if anybody denies it, I have the trade reports here to show that I am correct. The trade reports for 1925 show that we imported, largely from the United States. $149,201,000 of agricultural .products which we could have produced on the farms of Canada, and we imported as well $236,000,000 of farm products, such as cotton, tropical fruits, bananas, pineapples, oranges and so forth, which we could not produce in Canada.

speechtext:
Now in regard to the Dyestuffs Act, another important protective measure still in operation. The act was passed in 1920 by the coalition government of which Lloyd George was Prime Minister, and this is the statement which I find in this work with regard to it:
In 1913 Germans' made 83 per cent of the world's total production of dyestuffs, and we took 90 per cent of our requirements from abroad. To-day, as a result of the war and of government action, we have a dyestuff industry which supplies 80 per cent of our needs. The dyes made are quite equal in fastness and brightness to German dyes.
Then they proceed in regard to the prices.
In June, 1921, it is stated, the average price of British dyestuffs was a little over 4s. 4d. per pound. In December of the same year it had fallen to 3s. fid. per ipound; in December, 1922, it was about 2s. fid. per pound; and in 1923 the average was down to about Is. per pound. These figures represent a reduction of more -than 75 per cent *in the price of dyestuffs within three years of the passing of the act.
Did the raising of the tariffs there increase the price of these goods? It lowered the price of them. Where is the tariff a tax? The Prime Minister on one occasion in this House stated that a tariff is alwaj-s a tax. How is it always a tax, if in other countries it can be shown, as I have shown, that in many cases where you raise the tariff and keep the market for your own producers you lower the price of the article concerned?
I wish to make one more quotation from this book, because it contains a germ of truth which I would like to present to the House. It is a quotation from a speech of Daniel Webster, addressing the United States Senate in 1846. Mr. Webster stood very high in the estimation of the people in the United States; he was considered one of the immortals of the country. He says:
Where there is work for the hands of men, there will be work for their teeth. Where there is employment, there will be bread. It is a great blessing to the poor to have cheap food, but greater than that, prior to that, and of still higher value, is the blessing of being able to buy food, by honest and respectable employment. Employment feeds, and clothes, and instructs. Employment gives health, sobriety, and morals. Constant employment and well-paid labour produce, in a country like ours, general prosperity, content, and cheerfulness.

The Budget-Mr. Manion
I again ask, are we to ignore the lessons of history because a minority of free traders and low tariff men in this country control the government at the present time? Even England has realized that trade is a battle for markets. She has realized that her imports are unlimited and that thus she is not a free trade country, because no country traded with her on the basis of her free trade policy. But by that principle of unlimited free imports she was throwing away her weapons, opening her gates to the enemy and discarding her negotiating power. She realized that the index of a nation's prosperity is not in external balance sheers, not in the reports of Finance ministers, but in the condition of the workingman's dinner table and his clothes line. Where in this budget is the workingman's dinner table or his clothes line improved? We do not find it has any place in the budget. What we need in Canada is large production, plenty of work and wages for the people; in other words, a policy of buying and selling among ourselves. It is not cheap goods that we need; it is work and wages for our people. Suppose the tariff reduction had lowered the price of automobiles by an average of $5 to $10 a year to the man who buys a car every four or five years, is it not worth $5 or $10 per annum to the citizens of the country to build a broad Canadian development on a solid foundation?
The budget proposes a reduction of the duty on tin plates, which I am informed will injure an industry just formed in Quebec. The tin plate industry in the United States is one of the best illustrations of what can be done under a tariff to build up an industry. In 1890 the United States produced 2,000,000 pounds of tin plates, which was a mere bagatelle oecause they imported about 1,000 million pounds. In 1913, twenty-three years later, they produced not two million but two billion pounds of tin plate-a thousand times as much-and the price had gone down.
Sir Gilbert Molesworth wrote a book on the tariff question advocating a tariff policy for England, pointing out that steel rails sold in the United States for $150 a ton in 1867 when they had no tariff, and in 1885, eighteen years later, when a tariff was placed on steel rails, the price had decreased from $150 a ton to $27 a ton.. Before the war the price in the United States was $26 or $27 a ton, after they had imposed a high tariff and afforded protection for the producer in the United States. He gave a list of 214 other articles which, with increased protection, had gone down in price 25 per cent under the high tariff. Let us do likewise in this country.
Let the people of Canada apply the Golden Rule of commerce to other countries-do unto other countries as they are doing unto us. Let us have a policy of Canada for the Canadians. Let Canadian industry, Canadian thrift and resourcefulness provide us with all that we need, instead of our promoting foreign industry and buying the products of foreign cheap productiod. The issue is clear for the Canadian people to decide and to make a final decision as to their destiny. It is up to the members of this House and the government of this country to abide by that decision. This in a nutshell is the issue before the people to-day: The people of Canada must decide whether, under the lower tariff or free trade policy which this country is following, we -are to become a mere adjunct of the United States, allowing others to exploit us, to manufacture our raw materials, our asbestos, nickel, pulpwood and electricity, into the finished products, allowing them to take $5,000,000 of raw materials and convert it into $50,000,000 worth of finished production and thus get employment for their labourers and the manufacturers the profits. In other words, are we to permit ourselves to become the dumping ground for cheap producing countries? Are we to become the hewers of wood and drawers of water, the miners of minerals and growers of grain for other countries and the recruiting ground for their artisans? That is the effect of the low tariff policy.

I was not trying to show she was going to try to raise it now. I was trying to show that She had ruined her farmers and agriculturists by taking the tariff off. If I were living in England I would advocate putting a duty on a lot of raw materials and raw products in order to build up agriculture in that country. But I am speaking for Canada and not for England; the people of England will have to decide that question for themselves. I was showing what will happen to Canada under free trade or under a low-tariff policy.
The people will have to decide whether or not they want a national policy of protection for all the different industries of this country, a policy of Canada for Canadians, which will develop our own natural resources instead of allowing others to develop them for us; which will keep our markets for our farmers of Ontario and Quebec and the other provinces; which will protect our workers against a system of low .exchange, of cheap labour, and of the low standards of living of the Orient and Europe; which will give stability,to the business of the country; which will open the factories which have been closed, which will give encouragement to the establishing of other factories; which will give traffic to our railways by giving them a chance to carry our raw materials and our finished product; which will give work to the workmen of our country; which will give opportunities to our boys and girls to stay at home and to indulge that noblest sentiment in the human breast, patriotism, instead of their being forced to go to the United States, the most highly protected country in the world, to earn a living-in a phrase, a policy which will give us a wide, universal development, which will lead Canada to become a happy, prosperous, and contented nation, which prosperity will bring back to our land the sons who have been exiled from it and will draw millions from other countries to fill our vacant spaces. To my mind the latter policy, the policy of protecting all the industries of Canada, agriculture, manufacturing, and all others, is the red-blooded courageous Canadian policy and that is the policy which the people of Canada should support.
Mr. Speaker, in closing, because of the attitude which I have taken, I intend to move the following amendment:
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
In the late general election campaign assurances were repeatedly given by the Prime Minister and other 
ministers of the crown that before further tariff changes were made an opportunity would be given industries affected thereby to be heard before an advisory board.
That such assurances were officially incorporated by the government in the Speech from the Throne of the present session in the following words:
"Changes in the tariff should be made only after the fullest examination of their bearing upon both primary and manufacturing industries and that representations requesting increase or decrease of duties should be made tihe subject of the most careful investigation and report by a body possessing the necessary qualifications to advise the ministry with respect thereto. A tariff advisory board will accordingly be appointed forthwith."
That such tariff advisory board was accordingly appointed.
And this House regrets that in the case of drastic changes announced in the budget such assurances have not been fulfilled.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I desire in the finst place, Mr. Speaker, to compliment the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) upon the clear, concise and businesslike statement Which he presented to the House a few days ago. An occasion of this kind has, though of course on a very much smaller scale, its counterpart in the annual meetings of the ratepayers of our municipal governments. The mayor and council meet the taxpayers at the end of the year and, to use the popular phrase, give an account of their stewardship. Similarly, each year the taxpayers of the Dominion await with considerable interest the statement of the Minister of Finance with reference to the financial condition of this country during the year immediately preceding. It is of interest on such occasions, in reviewing the past, to contemplate also the proposals for the ensuing twelve months, and the taxpayers are always eager to ascertain whether or not there is likely to be any lightening of the burden of taxation.
The country generally received with some surprise and with a great deal of satisfaction the minister's statement, whidh is now being considered, wherein he showed that not only had expenditures been kept within the limits of revenues during the year just past, but that those expenditures had been so carefully curtailed and the business of the country so economically administered by this government that the very handsome surplus of some
S33.000.000 was achieved. This statement i3 gratifying indeed to the taxpayers of Canada. And following upon that the country received, probably with greater astonishment, the intimation that for the ensuing year there was

The Budget-Mr. Donaghy
to be a considerable diminution in the burden of taxation as disclosed by the resolution moved by the Minister of Finance. Perhaps the greatest and most outstanding act of administration since the days when the war clouds first loomed over Canada has been the much needed reduction in income tax which has been depressing business in this country for some years. The extent of the reduction in income taxes is striking, and in view of our present financial condition it would seem that we have gone as far as we can in that direction for the time being. For example, a man with a wife but no children and with an income of $3,000 per annum will pay no taxes whatever under the new schedule, while the same man, if he receives $3,500, will pay the trivial sum of $10 in taxes. Surely no one can complain of taxation assessed on that basis.
As regards the tax on incomes derived from dividends from shares held in corporations, a change has been made. The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) this afternoon offered some criticism in this regard. Heretofore the income received from dividends paid to the individual as a holder of dhares in a company was not taxable. Was that right? Was it fair that the income produced by toil and labour should be taxed while income so easily secured from capital should escape taxation?

speechtext:
Does the hon. member
mean to tell me that such dividends were not taxed?

.gentleman was not carefully following my words. If he will consult Hansard he will see what I said.
