speechtext: Answer the question.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
T do not like to repeat too often. If my hon. friend will listen carefully he will get the drift of my remarks and discover what the change is. The income tax upon the profits of corporations has also been reduced. Heretofore that tax has been ten and a half per cent over and above the first $2,000 of income and it has now been reduced to nine per cent, a reduction of approximately fifteen per cent. The income tax in the United States on the profits of corporations is higher than that; it is thirteen per cent. One of the great objections to this form of taxation is that it discourages investments in the industries of the country. [DOT] I am glad to see that the government has borne this principle in mind in drafting the resolution. We stand to-day in a more favourable position for attracting capital than does the United States.
Their income tax on the profits of corporations is, as I have said, thirteen per cent, and at the end of 1926 it will be increased to thirteen and a half per cent, while ours will remain at nine per cent. So that we shall be in an advantageous position as compared with our neighbours to the south. As I say, this budget resolution places us at an advantage because our taxation on income from investments is less than that of the United States, although ours on personal earnings is higher than theirs.
Another reduction in taxation which the country welcomes, and which probably was not expected this year, is the return to penny postage. The difference between paying three cents and two cents upon letters is of considerable importance to the population generally, especially to the poor. True, it is a small amount in itself, but in the aggregate it means a substantial saving to our people. Penny postage was made popular many years ago and after a great fight it became almost universal, but owing to war conditions it had to be abrogated. The return now to this popular rate of postage is another indication that financially Canada is fast moving out from under the clouds in which she has been enshrouded since the beginning of the war.
If there was one thing more than another that caused Canadians to look with some discouragement upon the future financial outlook of the country it was the annually recurring deficits on the operation of the Canadian National railway system. We have a similar problem to-day in British Columbia, where our provincial railway is being operated at a loss. It is a grave problem to my province. On a much more magnified scale the operating loss on our national system has been a source of much worry to those handling the finances of the Dominion for several years past. I do not think any of us were optimistic enough to expect that the serious operating deficits of from fifty to fifty-five million dollars annually, to which by their steady recurrence we were becoming accustomed, would so soon drop down to the comparatively small figure of a trifle over seven million dollars. The hope that even this deficit will soon be wiped out is, I am sure, shared by all members of this House, regardless of their political affiliations. It was particularly gratifying to hear the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) state last Thursday that this improved condition was a very encouraging sign, and I think he went so far as to say that there was every reason to expect the national railway system would be upon a paying basis within a very few years.
To a considerable extent discussions on the budget and on the Speech from the Throne

The Budget-Mr. Donaghy
invariably revolve around the tariff. It may be questioned whether too much importance is not attached to the annual debate upon tariff matters, and whether the two sides which battle so strenuously on this subject do so with any very deep sincerity. The history of our tariff legislation for the last twenty-five years shows practically no difference in the various tariff schedules, beyond a point or two, whether the administration was Liberal or Conservative. That bald fact has a tendency to make outsiders think that the range of debate in this controversy does not produce any very fruitful results. Let me say this: the discovery of Marquis wheat has resulted in the production of more wealth for Canada than all the discussions on the tariff that we have had since confederation. I might say the same with respect to the discovery of a new process for treating refractory ores. There are other things of importance besides the tariff worthy of consideration by this House. I welcome the announcement that a tariff board has been appointed. The tariff is too intricate and complex a subject for the people generally to understand and decide. I doubt even if many hon. members could pass a satisfactory examination on the tariff of this country. Some hon. gentlemen talk very learnedly of what the United States tariff is against our goods. This afternoon I heard an hon. gentleman on the other side state quite positively that the tariff on Canadian automobiles entering the United States was 50 per cent.

speechtext: I never said so at all. I never mentioned Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I said an hon. gentleman so stated. I think we all heard it on this side. The statement was a striking illustration of what I have already said, that a great many members of this House would not pass anything like a satisfactory examination on tariff matters, either regarding the tariff of their own country or that of the adjoining republic, whose praises are so loudly sounded by hon. gentlemen on the other side. Unfortunately for the hon. member who made that remark, the tariff on Canadian automobiles entering the United States is exactly the same as the tariff on United States automobiles entering Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
The Finance
Minister does not say so.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
The basis of the tariff on automobiles entering the United States is a duty of 25 per cent. Hon. members will find that in Vandegrift's United States Tariff,

1922, at page 70, paragraph 369. Let me read it:
Automobiles, automobile bodies, automobile chassis, motor cycles, and parts of the foregoing, not including tires, all of the foregoing whether finished or unfinished, 25 per centum ad valorem.
Then a proviso is added to the effect that if any country raises its tariff against United States automobiles higher than that point, the United States tariff against such a country will be raised accordingly.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Why don't you read it?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
That supports the assertion I made a moment ago, and which some hon. gentlemen opposite challenged. Our duty on automobiles was 35 per cent, and automatically under the article I have just quoted the United States raised their tariff up to the same point, so until the resolution was brought down the other day, the tariffs of the two countries on automobiles was exactly the same, namely, 35 per cent.
Coming back to the question of the most scientific way of dealing with the tariff, I must say that the wisest course seems to have been adopted this year of appointing a tariff board to inquire into tariff matters. In my opinion this board should have been appointed twenty years ago. We would then have had the benefit of a board devoting its whole time to the study of this question in an expert manner, and figuring out the consequences that might result from raising or lowering any particular item. But instead of that, the question of the tariff had been thrown into the political arena at every election, and about four weeks of very florid oratory has been devoted in every election campaign to educating the people of this country on the subject of the tariff. At a time like that, when their minds are excited by the heat of political battle, no good results, no logical conclusion, can ever be looked for from such a proceeding.
In connection with the action that has been taken regarding the duty on automobiles, the criticism may be offered that this action is inconsistent with the general policy of referring tariff matters to a tariff board. It is quite true that the action that was taken could not be justified on any consistent principle, but nevertheless it may and will be justified by the exigencies of the circumstances and of the case.

so big and fat and prosperous that its profits and its wealth are such as to shock the public conscience of the people of Canada. That is quite conceivable, and we have had probably the most glaring example of that which it ic possible to conceive of in any country in the Canadian Ford Company. Here is an industry protected to the extent of 35 per cent, the whole of which duty it milks and takes from the pockets of the taxpayers of this country, every dollar, and the company waxes so big and fat and pays such extravagant dividends, that the conscience of those who have not been so fortunate as to walk in these golden pathways is shocked at the necessity of keeping the milk bottle constantly at the mouth of this plutocrat. This had been probably the most glaring instance in Canada, and I am not astonished at all that public opinion has revolted and demanded that this condition be remedied by parliament, and remedied now, instead of a year from now. Every rule is proved by the exception, and the rule that a tariff board is the proper body to study and advise on tariff matters is proved by the exception in the case of the Canadian Ford Company.

There are two other matters which probably enter more into the question of the industrial development of Canada than the question of the tariff. One of those matters is the necessity for a fair and equitable adjustment of the freight rate structure all over this Dominion. That adjustment is more important than the tariff. We have heard a good deal on this subject in parliament during the past two months. We have heard the members from the Maritime provinces complain that the coal of Nova Scotia cannot at present freight rates be hauled to central Canada. They also complain that the ports on the Atlantic coast are not being used to the extent to which they should be used for the handling of Canadian grain. We have heard the same complaint regarding the ports on the Pacific coast, and we have heard the complaint that owing to the high freight rates coal from Alberta cannot be shipped to central Canada. Canada being so vast in extent, comprising as it does so many thousands of miles from ocean to ocean, is an exceedingly difficult country to govern and govern justly in order that hardships may not be imposed upon one section of a country more than upon another. There is nothing which will help more greatly to equalize the conditions of the people and the industries in the various parts of the country than a fair and equitable adjustment of the freight rate structure throughout the whole of Canada. The grain growers of the prairies desire low freight rates on their grain so that they may get that grain to the ocean and to the world's markets on a competitive basis with grain from some other country. On the other hand those who live in the cities and ports on the seacoast desire to see Canadian grain go through those ports and to see merchandise imported into Canada come directly into those ports. It i3 a matter for gratification that the government has taken another step in the latter direction. As a result of that step we understand that after the end of the present year it will be necessary that imported goods, in order to enjoy the full British preferential tariff, shall enter direct through a Canadian port. This is a step in the right direction. We should encourage the shipping of both exports and imports through our own ports.
The government, in my opinion, has taken proper steps during the past six or eight months for the equalization of the freight rates and the solution of the great problem involved. We find that on June 5, 1925, it passed an order in council which in part reads as follows:
The committee therefore advise that the board be directed to make a thorough investigation of the rate structures of railways and railway companies subject to the jurisdiction of parliament, with a view to the establishment of a fair and reasonable rate structure, which will, under substantially similar circumstances and conditions, be equal in its application to all persons and localities, so as to permit of the freest possible interchange of commodities between the various provinces and territories of the Dominion and the expansion of its trade, both foreign and domestic, having due regard to the needs of its agricultural and other basic industries, and in particular to:
(a)	The claim asserted on behalf of the Maritime provinces that they are entitled to the restoration of the rate basis which they enjoyed prior to 1919;
(b)	The encouragement of the movement of traffic through Canadian ports;
(c)	The increased traffic westward and eastward through Pacific coast poTts owing to the expansion of trade with the Orient and to the transportation of products through the Panama canal.

The Budget-Mr. Donaghy
Subsequently, on January 7, of the present year, an order was passed by the government which reads as follows:
The committee of the Privy Council therefore recommends that the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada be directed, as a part of the general rate investigation above referred to, especially to inquire into the causes of Canadian grain and other products being routed or diverted to other than Canadian ports, and to take such effective action under the Railway Act, 1919, as the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada may deem necessary to ensure, as far as possible, the routing of Canadian grain and other products through Canadian ports.

It is first of all desirable, so far as is practically possible, that the great stores of raw material which this country possesses in such vast degree should be manufactured in Canada; these resources should be worked up in Canada by Canadian workmen and give employment to our own people. In pursuance of that general principle and policy the government negotiated a very favourable commercial agreement with our sister dominion, Australia, under which

the newsprint of Canada is admitted into Australia on favourable terms. We know that in the year 1920 Canada lost the Australian market for its paper products. In that year Australia gave Great Britain a preference of $15 per ton on British newsprint. That shut Canada out of the Australian market. Through the efforts of this government, however, in negotiating a commercial treaty with Australia, Canada has now been admitted to the markets of Australia on these specially favoured terms so that her paper enters free as against a duty of $15 per ton on the newsprint of other countries. The newsprint industry of Canada is only in its infancy, but it will not be many years before it will be one of the greatest industries in this Dominion. We probably have in Canada the greatest stand of timber in the world to-day. Is it not desirable that through the negotiation of treaties opening up markets we should be enabled to manufacture the products of our forests at home in Canada and give employment to our own workingmen? One of these manufacturing processes is the working up of the rough product of the forest into newsprint. But what is the use of doing that if you have not got markets for the product? The first step to take is to find ia market. Having found a market, as we have for newsprint, the manufacturing of it at home by our own workmen naturally follows. We have a very good example of that in the province of British Columbia. About 100 miles north of Vancouver there is the town of Powell River, which is entirely a paper-manufacturing community of some 4,000 inhabitants. As a result of this treaty that company is now installing a new machine and doubling its capacity. Although that is an American concern, very few Americans are employed in it, and approximately 40 per cent of the workmen employed in that paper mill industry are veterans of the Great war, men who fought in France. What is_ the outlook in Canada for the future in the papei industry? The programme to-day of the Canadian paper industry is the installing of eighteen new additional machines. What is the programme of the world? For England the programme for the remainder of the year is the installing of one new machine, and for Finland one new machine. That is the world programme. Canada stands out preeminently over the other countries of the world in the programme she is outlining for the manufacture of newsprint. Shall we not go on and multiply treaties of this kind if possible, negotiate them wherever they can be negotiated on favourable terms, in order that the

The Budget-Mr. Sutherland (N. Oxford)
raw material of this country can 'be manufactured at home and industries built up in Canada on a sound commercial basis, utterly regardless of this wrangle we have every year in regard to protection?
We have this tariff with us; we have had it with us since we were children, and it will be with our grand-children. It is here to stay. History shows that. There is no use trying to deceive the public in regard to this matter. Notwithstanding the very heated and learned debates that we listen to between the various parties in this House, history still remains and the cold fact still stares us in the face that this good old tariff has never changed more than one or two points under any administration. The way to build up a country and its industries and to "create employment is not by wasting time debating the question; it is by going out and negotiating commercial treaties and finding i market for our raw products manufactured in Canada. The treaty with the West Indies is another example of that, and I have no doubt, if the government uses good judgment and is industrious and energetic, we will be able to multiply the favourable treaties as the years go by. We cannot get them all in one year. It is particularly commendable to note that the treaties negotiated in recent years have been made with our sister dominions. That is a very favourable outlook. We may look forward in the near future to the circle being increased, and later on we may possibly take in with our treaties, all the dominions forming the great British Empire.
I know it is not usual for a member upon his first appearance in the House to take up a great deal of time, and I have spoken long enough. I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and hon. members of this House, for the courteous hearing you have given me.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman who
has just resumed his seat (Mr. Donaghy) who has an acute legal mind which we have seen functioning in a fearful and wonderful manner at the customs probe, has given us a very good speech to-night; particularly did that legal mind come into play when he endeavoured to explain the exigencies of the situation which necessitated that the government should not direct the attention of the tariff board to the automobile industry. Apart from that, the hon, member made a very good protectionist speech, such as I am sure his protectionist constituents in Vancouver North will welcome.
I have understood that the discussion on the budget generally takes rather a wide range, and all sections of the country present their views in regard to matters which particularly affect them. This, I take it, is an exceedingly good thing, particularly for new members in the House, of whom we have a large number. It gives them a chance to widen their viewpoints and see what is going on in other parts of the country, and it also leads one to realize that this country must be governed by a policy in which there is a good deal of give and take. The hon. gentleman could not bring himself to one thing-he could not defend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) in the situation that was brought up in the House this afternoon, when we saw the spectacle of a minister of the crown endeavouring to change the meaning of what he said under oath out in the province of Saskatchewan. That is a thing that I do not think any minister has ever been known to do in this House before. There is also the spectacle of a minister being exposed, when it was clearly shown that he went up to the riding of West Middlesex and gave details of a conversation with another member of this House, which conversation never took place at all. We have heard a good deal from members on the other side of the House about stocks going up in this country since this government came into power. What has happened to-day certainly will send down the stocks of the hon. Minister of Railways in this country and in this House. I venture to say that had these facts been known to the government, even this government, brazen as it is, would not have asked him to sit in council with them.
I wish to continue what I was saying about the different parts of the country having different viewpoints. We have heard a good deal about the coal industry since we have been here, particularly from our friends from the Maritime provinces, and there is no doubt whatever that upon the proper solution of the coal problem depends a great deal that is very important to Canada as a whole. In the report of the provincial royal commission which was made last year, a former member of this House. Mr. Hume Cronyn, in an illuminating addendum to the report, sets out clearly what the rest of the country must do to solve or help to solve this fuel problem. He says that federal assistance towards the establishment of coking ovens must be given or, second, that there must be a substantial increase in the import duty on all bituminous and anthracite screened coal. In the budget

2642	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Sutherland (N. Oxford)
that was delivered the other day no assistance was given to the coal miners of Nova Scotia, and the reason advanced was that the matter had been referred to a commission and therefore was under discussion and Should not be dealt with by parliament. In spite of that the question of the tariff on automobiles is being dealt with in this House without being referred to a commission for investigation.
Another matter on which I wish to touch, because it enters very closely into the questions of the day, is the question of immigration. My views on immigration may differ from those held by many others. I believe in our present situation in Canada the cities should be built up ahead of the rural districts and our endeavours should be directed towards that end, because we would thus give more employment and a bigger market to the people in the rural districts. I realize that it would be folly to bring people to the cities unless we had work for them to do. The main problem, therefore, is to provide work in our cities, to bring the people in and to build up our urban population; that is what Canada needs far more than an increase in the number of farmers to settle on our land when our farmers now, according to some of them, are having hard work to make a living. The idea of bringing in mo're farmers is being advocated more by the farmers in this House than by others, and it is the only instance within my knowledge of an industry, which is complaining of hard times, urging and welcoming more competition for itself. That does not seem to me to be logical. In my opinion the cities should be built up first.
Another reason for my contention is this, that from year to year there is very little difference in the quantity of food products that are used throughout at least that part of the world that we have to do with. There is very little increase in population and, therefore, very little need for our farmers to produce more stuff. The situation in the cities is very different. More kinds of manufactures are coming to the fore every minute and there has been a tremendous development even in the last thirty years. The whole automobile industry, the phonograph industry, the radio industry and many other new kinds of manufactures are employing much more labour and that will be the case from now on. We shall therefore have more room for employment for the people in the cities as long as we have a proper fiscal policy that will provide work for them there.
A great deal has been said about the word "protection," or "safeguarding," as it is called

in some countries. I am firmly of the opinion that on that system of protection depends to a great extent the prosperity of Canada. When I speak of protection I mean simply protection; it is something that does not need to be qualified by an adjective "high," "low," "moderate," or anything of that kind. If you protect an industry, protection is all it wants, and it is superfluous to say "high," "low" or anything else. It is simply protection this country needs; if it has that it will get along all right.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) in his address laid a great deal of emphasis on the balance of trade as regards our dealings with the rest of the world, and he cited figures that were in a way very satisfactory. Our main dealings are with the United States, and according to the latest available figures, which take us up to the end of February of this year, we have a very large adverse balance in our dealings with the United States. In this year, 1926, we have imported from the United States $123,035,937 worth of stuff more than we exported, and in 1925 we imported $97,393,324 worth more than we exported. That shows that our adverse balance of trade with the United States is getting larger, in fact being more than $25,000,000 worse this year than last year. If this policy of cutting the protection from the automobile manufacturers goes into force and many of these cheaper cars are brought in from the United States, that adverse balance will be materially larger than it is now.
This budget as a whole is what might be termed a Saskatchewan budget. That statement deserves a little explanation. The general policies in Saskatchewan seem to be policies of annihilation and assassination rather than protection, and if
9 p.m. those members from Saskatchewan who seem to favour those policies get any more power in the House than they have shown they have, there is going to be very serious trouble for this country. The reason why I attribute this to Saskatchewan is, as the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) said this afternoon, because no reference was made in the Speech from the Throne to this reduction in the tariff on automobiles. I attribute this reduction more to Saskatchewan Liberals even than to our Progressive friends and I base this statement on part of a letter written by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) to his home paper about February 5, when he said:
The Speech from the Throne reassures the manufacturers by announcing that further changes in tariff duties are undesirable.

The Budget-Mr. Sutherland (N. Oxford)
This shows that the caucus which has been carried on and the conferences which had been held between the Liberal government and the Progressive executive had not at that time discussed and decided upon this question. What happened between that time and the present? Only this, that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was forced to leave Ontario and go to Saskatchewan for a seat and the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) left Saskatchewan and came down-to Ottawa to take a seat in the cabinet. Those two moves are the explanation of this tariff change. I do not think any reasonable person throughout Canada can bear out the stand of the government in this matter. I do not really think the Quebec Liberals, to a certain extent, bear out this stand, because I have noticed for the last two or three days that whenever there is any applause on the other side on account of the budget, the Liberal members applaud income tax reductions and the Saskatchewan members applaud reductions in the tariff on automobiles. That shows what the feeling of the House is on the matter.
During the debates that have been going on in this House almost since the beginning of the session we have heard a great deal from nearly every province as to its own particular question, Quebec being the only exception. Practically no one from the province of Quebec has risen in his place and told the House what are the main questions in which that part of the country is interested. There is a representation from Quebec of sixty-five members, sixty-one of whom are on the other side; yet we have heard practically not one word regarding the problems of that province.

That question presents no difficulty to me. I am in favour of preferential trade within the empire. I am absolutely for such trade and, I repeat, the question does not bother Conservatives. Every time we have a chance to buy something which cannot be made here I say, buy it from the United Kingdom or from any other part of the empire rather than from the United States or any other foreign country.
Now, I come to the subject which is of special importance to my own constituency, namely, farming. My riding is largely agricultural. We raise a lot of first class stock in the riding and any gentleman from Saskatchewan who has a black and white cow which he prizes, if he traces its ancestry back, will probably find that the original stock came from the county of Oxford. In milk and milk products we have played an important part in the country. In the county of Oxford the Toronto City Dairy has three large plants, Neilson's of Toronto have one large plant, as have the Canadian Milk Products Company and some other concerns, and there are as well a number of country butter and cheese factories. So anything that affects the dairy industry of the Dominion is very seriously felt in that riding. And the dairy industry in that county has been adversely affected by the Australian treaty, which the hon. gentleman who preceded me (Mr. Donaghy) lauded to the skies. In this connection I have a couple of resolutions from cheese and butter factories in my riding which I desire to place on Hansard. It will be realized that these resolutions reflect the opinion of a large number of milk producers who are the patrons of these cheese and butter factories. The first is from the Bright Cheese and Butter Manufacturing Company, Limited:
That we patrons of Bright Cheese and Butter Manufacturing Company a.t our annua] meeting do protest against the Australian treaty, in that it does not afford the dairy interests of the Dominion the protection enjoyed by other manufacturing concerns in Canada.
Therefore we would ask a speedy repeal of this unfair measure; and that a copy of this resolution be forwarded to the Minister of Agriculture, Ottawa.
The other resolution is from the East Zorra and Blandford Cheese Manufacturing Company, Limited:
Resolution passed at tlie annual meeting, March 1, 1926.

For over forty years we had the advantage of our distinguished leader, the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who during that time was the dominating figure in the public life of Canada. I remember during my first three sessions of parliament whenever I saw that great man rise in his seat to address the House I was reminded of two other distinguished men, William Ewart Gladstone and Abraham Lincoln. If we to-day will remember those illustrous men, Laurier, Lincoln and Gladstone, we will not go far amiss in doing our duty as public men.
In the province of Quebec we have a contented and happy people who believe in adequate protection-not in protection simply for protection's sake, to make a few people exceedingly rich at the expense of the masses. We believe that this great country with its diverse interests must be a country of give and take. In the last parliament there were as many free trade speeches from the extreme east as from the extreme west. We have the interests of the Maritdmes at heart in this House. I have heard it said on the opposite side of the House that the last parliament had no exponents of Maritime rights, but we who sat in the last parliament know differently. speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen need not laugh, because I am going to indulge in a crack at the automobile. I said to this gentleman, "I will give you a cheque up to six figures." He replied "All right; I will get a taxi and come up and see you". I said to him, "If you get a taxi you cannot do business with me. You can walk to my room in less than three minutes and if you do so the cheque is yours". Think of a man wanting to ride in an automobile for such a short distance! That is an illustration of the absurd things people will do.
The hon. member for Southeast-Grey (Miss Macphail) was talking about old age pensions one day. Like myself she comes from a rural section, but while I was born in the fifties she was not. But she understands that a little money can be made to go a long way if you have a little brain and are accustomed to frugal living and right habits. The leader of the opposition belittled the pension of |20 a month. Why, $20 a month was too small 1 How could a poor man with a family of eight or ten children feed that family and clothe and educate them? Well, those of us who were 'born in the fifties were not very sparing of the soles of our shoes but we were sparing of the seats of our pants. But the leader of the opposition says that twenty dollars a month is a mere bagatelle and far from sufficient.
I take this opportunity of speaking to-night because in this budget we have a wide scope and a wide range of subjects to deal with I fully agree that the hon. member for Southeast Qrey (Miss Macphail) was perfectly right in saying that $20 a month is sufficient to alleviate the wants of anyone who is sixty or seventy years of age. They would live frugally. Of course they say that necessity was the mother of invention in those days and people succeeded in living on a very small sum because they worked hard and lived frugally. I 
do not know what conditions will be like fifty years from now; probably $60 a month would not be an adequate allowance to live upon. The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) asks why this sales tax was not taken off two or three years ago. I would remind him that this government assumed a tremendous burden when it came into power. Great deficits were accruing year after year Three years after the war they had not been able to stop the deficits. When this government came into power the Canadian National Railways were in the worst possible condition, and the Prime Minister, a student of the great Sir Wilfrid Laurier, whose judgment he had imbibed into his being, searched the country for a man large enough to run the railway. He found Sir Henry Thornton, the greatest man available in the world for the job. Sir Henry was criticized in this House in 1921 and 1922, but not so very long ago opinion in regard to him began to change, and broadminded men throughout Canada, who perhaps had formerly criticized Sir Henry came to realize that he was fully capable to assume charge of the road. Time has proven that Sir Henry Thornton is big enough and has a scope and breadth of mind sufficient to enable him to carry on the system. I expect that within two years he will be able to show a surplus on the Canadian National and if the railway is-not able to pay dividends it will at least pay expenses and wipe out the deficit. Hon. members have criticized the government within the last few days because the burdens on the people were not being lifted, but the government is now taking action which will have the result of improving conditions and making business more prosperous.
I desire to tell hon. members what the government has done and to tell them why there is a third party in this House. The Progressive party was formed some years ago, with men of strong character who had a determined idea that the great west needed representation in this House-and they have procured it. If there is a third party in the House it is because the Union government were not sincere and would not make it fifty-fifty with the other side when that government was formed, but wished to keep the iron hand of Toryism over the administration; they would not stand for a fusion with the other side. The most able men in the Conservative party thrust out their clenched fist in denunciation of the Progressive party; they had no use for them and their ideas. In 1921 a large representation from the Progressive party was sent to parliament. They did not need to read their speeches when they got on their feet, although I do not think they had the-

The Budget-Mr. Baldwin
training of some other men who come here and read speeches prepared by somebody else.
I consider it a compliment to have the members of the Progressive group in this House.
What means I possess are all invested in industry in this country. I have an interest in the industrial world, and I would not make one change in the tariff to injure industries. I have heard the former member for Marquette, Mr. Crerar, the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) and other Progressive members in this House state several times that they did not desire to injure one legitimate industry in this country. That is a meritorious attitude on their part, and that is the most that the people of Quebec want. We want a country where people can live cheaply, a country to which people can come and realize that they have a glorious place to live in. Some years ago, when a boy from New England and a boy from Canada would meet, they would discuss matters with each other. One would say to the other, " What did you pay for your hat?" The other would tell him, and it would be shown in those days that everything was in favour of the boy residing in the United States. The result was that that boy would persuade his brother to leave Canada and go there. We believe that with our great water-powers and our great industries in Canada that we can keep this country a good place to live in and educate our boys; and that is what we wish to do. But if the poor man and his wife cannot have a little butter on their bread, they will complain. It took two sessions to stop the importation of oleomargarine, which was sold in Canada in competition with the farmer's butter. Some years ago a bill on this subject was presented to parliament by the Minister of Agriculture, and only seven Tory members supported it. Last year people came into my constituency and said the Australian treaty was going to destroy the farmers. Of course it was not the farmers they were particularly solicitous about; they wanted to destroy the Liberal party, and particularly myself. They went to a creamery in the community, operated by a man of intelligence, and they tried to scare him. I heard a swashbuckling legerdemain fellow telling the farmer, " You will never sell your cows in this country; you had better get out." The farmer said, " What is the matter?" The fellow said, " Oh, it is the Australian treaty." I said to him: "You are in the civil service and perhaps it would be as well for you to keep quiet. One thing sure is that you never earn your daily bread; you are a loafer, a parasite on the public. Now you are trying to scare the farmers to death as regards something that
will not materialize." What was the result? This butter maker said to that Tory: "This government has done more for the farmer by repealing the Oleomargarine Act than all you can do or say, and no butter will come six or seven thousand miles and be six or seven weeks in coming here." What was the result? Butter has advanced in price from thirty-eight cents a pound, and you could not buy a pound of butter until ten days ago in this city for less than fifty cents.
The hon. member for Fort William said this afternoon: All you want to do is to stick to power. It is a pretty good thing to stick to what you have. We are sticking here and we will not surrender the reins for four or five years at least. You tell us that we are usurpers. What would you do if you were over here? You are in the minority; you could not get anywhere. There is no foundation for the insinuation that this country is going to the dogs when one considers the condition it was in when we came into power. You found the treasury full of money in 1911 when you won this country by misrepresentation and flag-flapping. Then you started to dismiss all the Liberals that were in office throughout the length and breadth of this great Canada of ours and you proceeded to frame an act for the outside civil service to entrench your appointees so that they could not be dismissed. You spent large sums of money in building armories which are used as places of amusement and dance halls, and this government has had to keep caretakers in them, keep them roofed and painted, and have them locked and unlocked when amusements are being carried on. In my constituency my opponent used them as great auditoriums when he had Patenaude out there and no crowd. Patenaude was supposed to be a spell-binder but he did not do the Conservative party any particular good. By the skin of his teeth he managed to get seats here for three or four or perhaps half a dozen of his followers.
Then you wanted to maintain militarism. I am against militarism. If we had 400,000 men overseas, they were disciplined over there for several years and no annual drill should be necessary in this country. It is a shame to call out for annual drill these old soldiers who were in the trenches and who know as much about war as Stonewall Jackson did, and no one else knew more about war than he did. I hope the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) will be in the House when the militia estimates come up and will give us as good a speech as she gave last year. The world now wants peace. We do not want wars; we do not want to keep up a military
26o0
The Budget-Mr. Baldwin

machine, and with those 400,000 men who received military discipline overseas, we should have no need for annual drill for the next two or three decades because those men are in this country already disciplined and will be ready in time of war. But I hope there will be no such thing as war. We have in this wonderful country to the south the Monroe doctrine. I know some of the military men will laugh when I say that doctrine will keep aggressors out of this country. Looking at a map the other day I felt it was not such a bad thing that the United States had a strip of land west of the Yukon and half the length of British Columbia. They would have to fight in order to keep off any Asiatics or anybody else who wanted to come over, and while I do not wish to hide behind anybody else's wings, I do not object to go through a turnstile because somebody else turns it. If this country is safe under the Monroe doctrine, it is as safe under that doctrine as under any other, but we do not want money spent in this country to keep up a military machine and nonsensical camouflage.
Perhaps in two months from now money will be appropriated for annual drill, although I hope not, and the farmers will be sent to Petawawa when they should be on the farms, when the crops need the most attention and the weeds grow fastest. I know a man who had several horses and he took his sons and his horses to the camp. When he returned home he found that potato bugs had eaten up $200 worth of potatoes and he got enough of his medicine in taking his horses up there to earn some money. If they want to drill, let them drill in October. In my time the drilling was done in October and the boys had to hustle in order to keep warm. Militarism, I repeat, is something we do not want.
As the hon. member for Fort William was speaking this afternoon I wondered if there was any love of country in Canada. I wondered if there were nothing here to make us patriots. I wondered if our rivers were not long enough, broad enough, deep
10 p.m. enough, rough enough or placid enough, to make us love our country. I wondered if our broad prairies with all their fertility were not enough to make, us realize that we have a great country in which wre should live in happiness. I wondered if the lofty mountains were not high enough to make one visualize the greatness of this country. I wondered if all our great mineral wealth, our great lakes and our fisheries were not enough to make us love our country and be patriotic. I wondered if there was not enough in the great topography

of this country, the vast extent of 4,000 miles east and west and nearly 2,000 miles north and south, to make us love it and not sit in this House and cavil and fight for the old parties. I wondered, if all these things could not make us love our country, if we had not better take a walk around this great structure which has risen from the ashes of the great devastation of the last House. We should be proud of this great structure and proud because we have in Canada the institutions that we have. When we walk around this great structure we should look at some of the monuments of our forefathers, the statesmen of this country who have built and built well, who travelled the stormy seas when it took six to eight weeks to cross the Atlantic, in order to break t'he family compact that was ruling Quebec and Ontario at one time. After we walk around this building and visualize the statesmen who hewed out the destiny of this country and laid the foundation and laid it well, we should have some love of country. It would indeed be surprising if anyone could fail to take an enthusiastic interest in the progress of th'is young and growing country after carefully studying its traditions and its institutions- our churches, our educational establishments, our philanthropic organizations of one kind or another, our great and ever expanding industry. There is in Canada everything that can inspire one to the loftiest patriotism, and if Canadians will only appreciate their great heritage there is no reason why, remaining within the British Empire, this country should not become one of the greatest nations on earth.
As regards the budget, I gather from the headlines in the newspapers that gentlemen opposite intend to fight the thing to a finish until the dog days come. Let me assure the opposition that the people of Canada are absolutely in favour of the proposals of the Minister of Finance. Speaking for the thrifty people in the Eastern Townships from which I come, I can say that the income tax reductions have received a hearty welcome. Why Should we not retain in Canada people who, being too old to continue in active work, have yet enough to retire upon? There is no sense in taxing such people and making it impossible for them to live in this country.
In connection with the reduction in the duties on automobiles, there is no doubt that the sentiment of the Canadian people is overwhelmingly in support of the government. I dislike the automobile probably as much as anybody else does, and I can quite understand the attitude of people in the country towards those who have made themselves wealthy out of this industry. They say, "We

The Budget-Mr. Baldwin
can go across the line and buy an automobile for one-third less than we can get it in Canada. We can get gasoline in the United States for one-third less, and we can obtain all the necessary accessories at a third of the price we have to pay in this country. Under the circumstances, why should we be compelled to pay exorbitant prices merely in order to provide profits for the manufacturers?"
The complaints of the manufacturers are not sincere; they are just so much camouflage. Surely they do not need so much protection in view of the profits they have made. In the past decade it has not been an uncommon thing to read in the obituary notices names familiar to everyone as descriptive of certain types of car-the names of men who have died worth tens of millions of dollars. Has anyone any deep sympathy with these people? There appears in the Montreal Herald to-day a cartoon which is really appropriate to the ipresent situation. There is a ponderous gentleman with a corporation of extraordinary proportions and beside him there is a figure supposed to represent the Minister of Finance who proposes to reduce his avoirdupois. I for one think that Henry Ford should be made to disgorge some of the wealth which he has accumulated through the oppressive measures that have been adopted by his organizations representing his business. I have known more than twenty men who have been ruined through acting as agents for the Ford corporation. These men sign contracts with the company and when cars are shipped and delivery is not taken, the agents are obliged to pay the demurrage. The only garage man I know of who is worth a 'lot of money has worked from sixteen to twenty hours a day and he has never signed any agreement with any company to sell cars. He finds people who, having mortgaged their homes or their farms to get cars, are unable to meet their payments, and he buys those cars for a fraction of what they were worth originally. He holds them for a little while and then disposes of them at a profit. Invariably the automobile organization is heartless. I do not say that Henry Ford is aware of everything that goes on, but certainly the organization that Represent him have been a curse to the country. There are thousands of vacant farm houses in the United States and Canada, the owners having failed to pay for the cars after mortgaging their places to get them. The trouble with people nowadays is that they are not satisfied unless they can make a great display. Long ago the farmer never thought of selling his buggy because it was old; he got it repainted or revamished.
To-day, on the contrary, when a man's car becomes a little shabby he immediately disposes of it and gets something more pretentious.
I notice that the hon. member for Fort William, as well as the leader of the opposition, has left the chamber. These gentlemen probably suspected that I had something to say to them, and so dleared *out. The hon. member who spoke for the Conservative party this afternoon indulged in a good deal of adverse criticism of the government. But what are the facts? When this government came into power our dollar was worth only eighty-three to eighty-five cents, whereas it has been at a premium practically half the time during the past eight months. This is due to the fact that as a result of proper administration the trade of the country has expanded. With the favoured nation agreements which we have entered into with certain countries, our export trade has advanced by leaps and bounds, and the country has every reason to be gratified. In view of this fact, the criticism of the hon. member for Fort William this afternoon came, I thought, with very poor grace. I do not want to make any speech of the boomerang type. The Australian boomerang is said to return to the one who throws it, and in like manner unfair criticism is apt to recoil upon the critic. I am bound to say, however, that it is a matter for great satisfaction to the government that no one has been able to point to any scandal during its administration. There has been no black sheep in the family on this side, and the government is possessed of brains enough to run the business of this country to the satisfaction of the people. The Liberal .party has never been governed iby the crack of the whip. We are free thinkers.
Some hon. MEMBERS. Oh, oh.

That is right. That is
the proper thing, so long as we think tfie administration of the country is what it should be. A party that servilely obeys the crack of its leader's whip is a party of slaves, and t'he Liberal party has never come within that category. Democracy will not tolerate it, and we will not tolerate it. For that reason, to-night I stand in defence of this budget. What has the merger done for Canada? The merger has gone out and bought up all the little factories, be they woollen mills, flour mills, iron foundries, or carriage factories, and amalgamated them into big organizations, but these have almost invariably failed because the merger did not take also the men of
The Budget-Mr. Messervy

genius who had founded and directed all those little local concerns throughout rural sections. That is the trouble with the merger of a lot of our industries. The merger fails 'because those behind it try to run the organization with a man in an office surrounded by a staff of stenographers.
Let our manufacturers wake up when they get up and 'they will find themselves able to withstand a lowering of the tariff. Indeed, they will be better fitted to carry on their business. One of the worst features of this country is that we are apeimg the habits of the United States. I hope my hon. friends opposite will take their medicine hereafter, whether bitter or sweet, with a smile. Let us do the business of this parliament without unnecessary delay and get out of here at least in the month of June.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, being a new member, I wish to congratulate you, sir, upon the high office to which both sides of this House have unanimously appointed you. You are courteous and kind, possess the best possible judgment, and are absolutely fair and impartial in your decisions.
I have, sir, the honour to represent Queens county in the province of Prince Edward Island. As my time has been entirely devoted to business I am unaccustomed to public speaking, but on behalf of the Conservative party I will endeavour to contribute what I can to the discussion of the various matters that enter into the public affairs of our country.
Let us look at the map of Canada, Mr. Speaker. Our country is divided by natural barriers into four parts. First, British Columbia, separated from the prairie provinces by the Rocky mountains. Second, the prairie provinces separated from the settled parts of Ontario by a large tract of rocky country in New Ontario. Third, the central provinces, nearly cut off from the Maritimes by the northern part of the state of Maine; and fourth, the Maritimes.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we may as well face the fact that there are certain difficulties in preserving the unity of all these parts, owing to long rail hauls through sparsely settled districts. The tendency, apart from nationalistic considerations, as has often been pointed out before, would be for each of these parts to trade with that portion of the United States directly south of it. And if we are to preserve Canada as a nation this tendency must be combated. It is no use complaining for instance, of railway deficits. We must of course run our National railway as economic-
ally as possible; but in doing this all services should be adjusted with the consideration first and foremost in our minds that Canadian ports, Canadian farms and Canadian industries are not to be suffered to languish, sicken and die, simply because, in the view of some shortsighted people, it is more economical to make use of United States ports, farm products or industries.
The unity of Canada is very ill served by starving one part into a state of discontent for paltry economic reasons. And, sir, this is the state of the Maritimes. In contrast with other parts of this Dominion they are actually losing in population. In view of this, it is nothing less than a disgrace that in winter and summer our grain is being shipped through Portland and other United States ports instead of through Halifax and St. John. Furthermore, there is need of considerable adjustment in the rates on coal between the Nova Scotia coal fields and central Canada. And we in Prince Edward Island would like to find a market for our potatoes in Ontario and Quebec. As it is, most of them go south even in the face of considerable duty.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I will consider in further detail these matters and other matters vitally affecting our welfare.- I am much interested in the question of Maritime rights and stand shoulder to shoulder with my Maritime friends in advocating the rights of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. The three have a combined area of less than 52,000 square miles and a population of about one million people. We have one forty-fifth of the area and one-ninth of the population of all Canada. We average twenty persons to the square mile, while the average of the other six provinces combined is four persons to the square mile. So, Sir, you can see that the Maritime provinces are an important unit in the Canadian confederation. The building up of a still greater Canada depends in a large measure on the development of the Maritime ports for commercial purposes.
Halifax has the best port in North America, and during the war it was used extensively for the moving of troops and exporting of foodstuffs to England. It has splendid docking facilities and a large grain elevator. It is a crime to pass this port for the shipping of grain for any port in the United States. It is the duty of the government to make it possible for shippers to use this port without loss to themselves. It is contended that the distance to Halifax is greater than to Portland, and other United States ports, and that freights are higher to Liverpool via Halifax than via United States ports. The Maritimes

The Budget-Mr. Messervy
claim it as a right that all Canada should help to lighten this burden for the building up of an all-C'anadian trade as well as to increase the prosperity of the Maritimes.
We have a splendid graded road of railway built on Canadian soil. The Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways have each a fleet of up-to-date steamers at their disposal. There is no valid reason why Halifax should not with St. John have a large wheat trade with Great Britain during the winter and summer.
Another matter that the Nova Scotia members should strive for is the making of Halifax a port of call for the largest and fastest steamers afloat, such as the Olympic and Mauretania, sailing between England and New York, and have them land, both on their inward and their outward voyages, passengers and mails during the winter and summer.
St. John is another port of great value to Canada. This port has the Canadian Pacific steamers calling during the winter months, and all the influence of the board of trade, the local government and city council, together with any other influence they can bring to bear, along with the influence of their members at Ottawa, should be used to get for the port of St. John her fair share of business. If the United States shipments of wheat were shut out, there would be sufficient quantities both in winter and summer to keep these ports busy as well as Montreal.
The coal company in Cape Breton is depending on increased sale of their coal in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. Mr. Speaker, I wish to call the attention of this House to the immediate necessity of the coal company erecting coal plants at Montreal, Toronto, Windsor, Fort William and other centres for the storage of coal, the installing of coke ovens, and, if necessary, the manufacture of by-products from the coal. During the summer months the coal company can rush large steamer cargoes of coal to Montreal. Smaller steamers and barges can carry cargoes of coal from Montreal as far west as Fort William. Large quantities of coal can be stored by the aid of cheap water rates, which will enable the coal company to compete and perhaps undersell the American companies to the manufacturing concerns in Canada, while the coke can be used for household purposes in Ontario and Quebec. To do this business, the coal company must have live, pushing, determined agents, and in this way I feel sure immense quantities of coal can be disposed of.	_	,
I would also urge, in connection with the operation of the West India treaty, the erection
of a canning and preserving plant in the Maritime provinces, because the West Indies require large quantities of canned goods, such as fish, peas, beans, potatoes, in fact, all kinds of vegetables, as well as fruit, berries, meats, soups, condensed milk and all kinds of poultry, also pickles. The farmers and fishermen of Prince Edward Island would benefit from the establishment of such a plant for they could ship to it large quantities of vegetables and fruit. It would in that way open up a new avenue of trade for us and be a great boon to our Maritime provinces.
At the time when Prince Edward Island entered confederation in 1873, we borrowed from the Dominion government 13,400,000 to pay for the railway which we had built. Adding interest at five per cent to this amount brings the total cost of this railway to date to $5,610,000. I do not think that any other province has had to pay for its railway accommodation in this manner. All have been provided for out of the general fund, and it is evident that we are entitled to be reimbursed for this $5,610,000. As one representative of the province of Prince Edward Island, I ask the government and parliament now for a refund of this amount, and I feel sure that the justice of our claim will be recognized.
The exodus from Prince Edward Island during the past three decades has reduced its population by upwards of twenty thousand people. Many of the youth of the island have left their native province to locate in western Canada and the United States. Those who go to western Canada are assisting in building up our great Dominion, and we offer no regrets for their loss, but when they leave us to locate under a foreign flag we feel the loss keenly.
We also want another car ferry steamer, and it should be an oil burner. Forty years ago, and previously, all our imports and exports had to be handled within the six months of comparatively mild weather. This was a necessity which business well understood and accommodated itself to. For a period of thirty years we had a winter service by means of ice breaking steamers running between Georgetown and Pietou, whereby not only mails and passengers, but a certain amount of freight, were transported, and during the latter twenty years of this period there were two winter steamers on this route.
With the advent of the car ferry service at the Capes, the whole export and import trade of the island has taken on a radical change. The import trade is now carried on in the winter pretty much as in the summer. The retail merchants and coal dealers no longer
The Budget-Mr. Messervy

find it necessary to lay in, in the summer and autumn, goods and supplies sufficient to do them till the following spring, for the car ferry steamer is kept busy all winter for almost six months in carrying the imports required for the business of the province. No coal or such kind of goods was ever imported on the winter steamers between Pictou and Georgetown. The export trade has also largely increased during the winter months, and will doubtless continue to increase with the coming years. The present service is of great advantage not only to business men, but to the farmers. While it enables the merchants to stock up with goods only as they require them, it also makes it possible for the farmers to export in the winter with almost as great a facility as in the summer. In this way both are benefited, the merchant in having less interest to pay than when he had to carry six months' supplies in goods, with the added advantage of being able to keep his store trim and attractive with supplies of fresh goods as needed, and the farmer in being able to sell his products in a strong market, thus the better enabling him not only to pay his bills to the merchant, but to buy more goods at his store. This is a state of things I wish to see continued, and not broken in upon by any want of attention on the part of this Parliament.
At present there is only one steamer available for service at the Capes. It i3 twelve years since she was built. Twelve years service has demonstrated improvements in construction which can be made in the building of a new steamer. The continuous and persistent fighting for years of heavy ice between the Capes must have done much to weaken and impair the present boat. If by any misfortune anything should happen to disable her during the winter season from performing the service for a fortnight, or even for a week the dislocation of business and the consequent loss, damage and inconvenience to a whole province would be difficult to estimate. Not only so, but to a people so dependent on imported coal it would entail great suffering, and it is therefore well to look ahead and take means to ensure against such a calamity.
Prince Edward Island is one of the most beautiful places in the world during the summer time. We have a splendid climate and lovely pastoral scenery. Once a tourist comes to Prince Edward Island he wants to come again, that i3, if he is not scared away by the difficulties and discomforts of the trip. If he comes by train he must leave his Pullman car at Sackville, change trains there, change again to get on the ship and again on leaving her. Now all this is very inconvenient and

unpleasant, especially for women with much luggage and possibly young children. In summer at least we are entitled to a through sleeping car operated from Boston or Montreal to Charlottetown, and the day coaches also should be taken over in the steamer, but as it seems that the steamer cannot handle these cars and at the same time bring over all the freight, this cannot be done at present. Our people are greatly interested in the great benefit to be derived from the cultivation and expansion of the tourist trade, and we have made substantial outlay in connection therewith. There is much in the construction and equipment of the present boat, and in the rail approaches thereto, to annoy and hamper that trade. Every motor car that goes to and from the island has to be loaded on a flat railway car and then hauled into the boat by means of an engine. If the driver of an automobile wishes to cross he must be at the station at Borden or Tormentine at least half an hour before the boat sails, and when he crosses he is kept in the boat usually for another half hour before the car can be hauled out in the same manner in which it came in. These restrictions are very annoying, and call for redress. A new boat so constructed as to permit autos to be driven by their own power on and off the vessel would be a great convenience, and would contribute powerfully to the success of the efforts of those of our people who are labouring so faithfully to interest tourists in our splendid climate, our charming scenery and our unsurpassed sea bathing. With great confidence I ask the government to place a sum in the supplementary estimates for the building of a new boat, which the other representative for Queens (iMr. Jenkins) has also asked for. Such a vessel is certainly needed. Furthermore,, as all hon. members well know, it will provide efficient communication between the island and the mainland, which is one of the terms of union on which Prince Edward Island entered the 'Canadian confederation.
Now, as to the products of Prince Edward Island. Last year the "million acre farm" yielded well, and the province fully maintained its reputation in the matter of farm products owing to the very large export of potatoes, including not only the seed stock, for which we are becoming justly famed abroad, but also tubers for the table. It is estimated that, about 1,500,000 bushels, valued at $1,875,000, were-shipped, including 350,000 bushels shipped through the Potato Growers' Association. The railroad had all it could do to handle
