An industry that we pride ourselves upon, and one which was started in Prince Edward Island, is the silver fox industry. Now, if we send a pelt to the United States we are charged a duty of 50 per cent, which means in the case of a pelt worth $300 a duty of $150. The United States are also engaged in breeding foxes, but while they dharge us a duty of 50 per cent they send pelts into our Canadian markets duty free. The inevitable result will be that they will surely capture those markets from us unless proper safeguards are adopted in Canada. At the Royal Winter Fair in Toronto foxes from Prince Edward Island, as usual, carried off all the prizes.
Now I come to deal with the question of freight rates. A great deal has been said about t'he unfair division of freight rates. I will give an illustration of how that works out. Oats and potatoes are among the chief articles raised in Prince Edward Island. If a shipper sends a carload of oats from Fort William to Sydney, a distance of 1,876 miles, he pays a freight rate of 62 cents per 100 pounds. To ship a carload of oats from Fort William to Halifax, a distance of 1,723 miles, costs 57 cents per 100 pounds. On the other hand the freight rate from Tignish, the most westerly point of Prince Edward Island, to Sydney, a distance of 436 miles, is 36i cents per 100 pounds; and from Tignish to Halifax, a distance of 294 miles, the freight rate is 30
The Budget-Mr. Messervy

cents per 100 pounds. As to export rates, the following will serve as an illustration:	A
shipper at Fort William sending products to Halifax intended for Newfoundland, the West Indies or Great Britain, enjoys a rate of 34 cents per 100 pounds. On the other hand on a shipment from Tignish to Halifax a freight rate of 30 cents per 100 pounds is charged, a notable discrimination in favour of the Fort William shipper.
The House can see the disadvantage under which Prince Edward Island labours. It will be apparent to any person how unfairly we are treated. This freight rate question must be settled on a more satisfactory basis if the Maritime provinces are to receive that measure of fair play to which they are justly entitled. I may point out that at the annual meeting of the Charlottetown Board of Trade it was stated that after much agitation throughout the Maritime provinces on this matter, Mr. S. C. Cornell had been engaged by the three lower provinces to investigate freight rates and questions relating to Maritime interests. This gentleman has already unearthed a good many difficulties which militate against Maritime prosperity. For example, the discovery was made very recently of a freight charge on potatoes extending a more favourable charge to southwestern Ontario than to Prince Edward Island. A submission has been made in this regard which has resulted in a partial remedy of the trouble. I am not going to enter into figures, because figures cannot be retained in the mind and they are subject to change from day to day. Let me impress upon the House, however, that the question of freight rates is a vital one in the province from which I come.
Dealing with the question of transportation, the Charlottetown Board of Trade enumerates the following amongst the needs of Prince Edward Island:
1.	The need of a second car ferry.
2.	The need of a longer continuation of the double mail and passenger service from and to the mainland.
3.	The need of a better local passenger service.
4.	The need of more railway yard room to handle the increasing export freight, at the time of the heavy movement of crops in the autumn.
5.	The need of a safe deep water terminus with better frost proof warehouse accommodation.
6.	The need of complete widening of the gauge of the railway of Price Edward Island.
7.	An improvement in the accommodation for transfer at Borden and Tormentine.
It is the conviction of many members of the board in question, particularly those who have been actively engaged on the time table and transportation committees, that the lately perfected Diesel electric passenger coaches

would go a long way towards solving our local passenger difficulties. It would seem to be obvious that so long as much of our local service is given by mixed freight and passenger trains, no really satisfactory service can be looked for. The introduction of Diesel electric cars would make it possible to separate freight and passenger trains and fnr each to give better service.
Although I am opposed to the government yet I must say that the establishment of a disease-free area in Prince Edward Island has met with general approval, and will no doubt accomplish much good. It is estimated that we have about 100,000 cattle in Prince Edward Island. About 55,000 of these are milkers; the others are young and beef cattle. Naturally in view of the favourable condition in which we are now placed these figures will tend to show an increase in the years immediately to come. We are proud that in this matter, as in several others, our province leads the rest of the Dominion in having become throughout its entire extent a disease-free area. The result of this splendid movement has been, of course, to promote a greatly increased demand for cattle from this area, a demand which we are not >ie>t able to meet. It is hoped that within a reasonable time our people will be able to realize on this demand and thus establish another permanent and splendid market for our products.
While referring to some of the many matters Which are of particular interest to our people, and which I feel it my duty to place before this House, I would like to point out that some months ago an American syndicate commenced experimenting by boring for oil on Governor's Island, situated a short distance from the mouth of the harbour leading into Charlottetown. The borings on that island, which is about one mile long and three quarters wide, have reached a depth of about 1,300 feet or more. Already there has been an outlay of about 1250,000 and it is estimated that a total of S300.000 will be expended. This provides employment for labour. It is quite a novelty in our province; and should the promoters strike oil there is no telling what a vast benefit there will be not only to Prince Edward Island but to the Maritimes provinces generally.
It will be of vital importance to the farming and fishing industry of Prince Edward Island, if one of our government merchant marines freight steamers with cold storage accommodation should make Charlottetown a port of call on the way to Great Britain. A splendid business could be worked up with sheep,

The Budget-Mr. Messervy
cattle, butter, cheese, eggs, hay, oats, lobsters, bacon and live hogs for the British market. The steamers now pass outside of Prince Edward Island; by going around the west end of the island to Charlottetown they would not be more than thirty miles out of the course that they take to Great Britain.
I would also request that merchants be not asked to guarantee space, but that it be advertised that a steamer will call at this port for Great Britain, say every two weeks going and coming. Our merchants can then send their travellers through the British Isles and work up business. At first one steamer could go to Liverpool, the next trip could be to Glasgow and the next to London, which would give them the choice of these three large markets, Manchester might be one of the ports, which is a very large market. This service would be of immense value for the farmers of Prince Edward Island, as they cannot compete now with the railway freight rates by sending their goods to Halifax, St. John or Montreal for shipment to Great Britain. Charlottetown is the capital of the province, and is entitled to this direct service. With the steamship service to Pictou, Nova Scotia, Magdalen Islands, Newfoundland, Sydney and Halifax, and with a direct steamer for Great Britain and the West Indies, Charlottetown will become quite an important port..
The bringing of steamers to Charlottetown would enable our longshoremen, labourers and truckmen to find work, and they want it badly. We have a splendid body of men forming our longshoremen's associations or unions. They work night and day, rain or shine, and deserve every encouragement. There is a steamship line now operating between Charlottetown and Pictou, and this gives a very valuable connection between Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia, Large amounts of freight have been moved by this line. We also have another steamship coming from Pictou, calling at Charlottetown, Souris and the Magdalen Islands, and this service is an excellent one, I think the best that has ever been provided. A first class steamer is on this route and makes regular trips during the summer months. We would like another steamship connection between Gaspe, Charlottetown, Summerside, Souris, Magdalen Islands and the Sydneys. This would be a very valuable connection to us because the steamer could bring coal on her return trip landing either at Magdalen Islands, Charlottetown, Summerside or Gaspe. I think a very profitable business could be worked up, and I would especially call Mr. Speaker's attention to this new service because he represents Gaspe and Magdalen Islands,.
I wish to mention some improvements that I would suggest in connection with the railway on Prince Edward Island. The Diesel electric line should be built, starting from Charlottetown, connecting with Tracadie, running along the shore to Brackley Beach, thence to Rustico, thence to Malpecque and into Kensington, connecting with the main line there. This would give splendid accommodation to our farmers at the outlying districts, and be of immense value to our fishermen at Rustico and all along the north side of the island-and I must point out to you that Rustico is one of the most valuable fishing grounds in Prince Edward Island. It would assist our fishermen to ship their fish by express quickly to the large cities, and would help them to build up this industry. A railway running along the shores of Richmond Bay between Malpecque and Kensington would tap immensely rich deposits of the finest mussel mud, which is a splendid fertilizer and is always in great demand among our farmers. There would be a splendid freight traffic over this line and worked, as it would be, by tihe Diesel electric locomotives, the operating cost would be very small. The line could be further extended along the south shore of the island from Borden to Charlottetown, thus supplying the farmers in this district with excellent fertilizer and bringing a valuable freight traffic as well.
I would strongly urge that the new railway shops that it is proposed to build at Charlottetown should be larger thaq the present ones. -We want to do more repair work on the cars-painting, woodwork, mechanical repairs and the like; we want more men employed there and fewer cars sent over to Moncton to be repaired. This work can be done as well as, if not better, art Charlottetown than anywhere else. We have the very best workmen there. In 1921 some of the Liberal candidates on the hustings promised that the railway shops would become a beehive of industry and would assist labour of all kinds, but the reverse has taken place. Our men have been discharged and work has been curtailed.
We also want our superintendent to have greater authority in purchasing and matters of that kind, and to be given full powers in every respect regarding the operation of the line from 'Sackville throughout the whole of Prince Edward Island. He has splendid ability and can do this as well as anyone. Moncton has entirely too much to say in the management of our Prince Edward Island railway.
I wish to urge the necessity of more yard room for docking and shipping facilities at the

265S

The Budget-Mr. Messervy
railway wharf in Charlottetown, and the enlargement of the frost-proof warehouse there; it is entirely too small. I understand the wharf has been condemned; steps should be taken at once to have it repaired. The road bed from Charlottetown to Souris and Georgetown, I understand, is ready for the widening of the gauge and this should be done the first thing in the spring, as our people are clamouring for the completion of the wide gauge railway on Prince Edward Island. Another important branch should have the gauge widened, namely, from Charlottetown to Murray Harbour. The present line goes through a splendid settlement, and it is only a narrow gauge railway.
In speaking of frost-proof warehouse accommodation at Charlottetown I would also recommend that you put a frost-proof warehouse at 'Souris, Georgetown, Borden and Summerside for this reason: in winter time, during the month of January, the whole of February and part of March, snow storms block the country roads and our railways for days, keeping our farmers from hauling their potatoes, especially in frosty weather. In the fall when they are taking potatoes from the ground they can store them in these frostproof warehouses, so that refrigerator or heated cars can be despatched during the winter mouths. The price obtained would then give splendid profit, thereby benefiting the people of Prince Edward Island and furnishing freight for the road when times are dull. I would earnestly urge upon the railway authorities to have the road bed well ballasted all over the island railway.
Our fishing industry is good. We have taken out of the waters this year about $1,500,000 worth, and we could quite easily make it $5,000,000 worth. We must remember that the people on the south side of Nova Scotia living near Lunenburg and La Have operate in fishing schooners in the spring of the year around our island, and then later on the Grand Banks. We can do the same. We could get together a fleet of vessels, place our products on the markets of the Mediterranean and South America, and work up a splendid business. An increase of our fishing operations would be of immense value to Prince Edward Island, giving employment to every kind of labour in connection with the building and fitting of vessels, and the curing and shipping of fish.
It is necessary, in order that all the available ports in Prince Edward Inland, may be utilized, to keep the harbours and rivers on the north and south shores of the island well dredged. The water accommodation thus

provided would give lower freight rates for the shipment of produce and the receiving of coal and lumber, our small vessels being enabled to enter and leave these harbours and rivers without grounding. Small harbours can also be dredged for fishing boats so as to allow our fishermen to prosecute the fishing industry more successfully. I would urge the Public Works department to place one dredge on the north side and the other on the south side of the island so that this work can be done quickly.
I	plead for lower freight rates for merchants along the line of railway who have to ship by cars all the year round from the several stations. Our ports are well located and we cannot complain about the water freight rates in summer, but for about five months of the year Prince Edward Island has very serious ground for complaint as to the high railway freight rates that prevail in the winter months, when we must ship and receive all goods by rail. *

I do hope that all hon. members on both-sides of the House of Commons will treat the-matter in a non-partisan light and charge the United States the same duties on the same kind of articles, especially farm products, as they exact from us. Is not this fair and equitable treatment from every angle and every point of view that you may argue?
I quote the following just to show the quick action of Canada in 1872. In 1872 Sir Francis Hincks, Minister of Finance in Canada, took off the 10 per cent duty on tea imported into Canada. In the same year the United States people put on a duty of 10 per cent on tea that was imported from countries west of the cape of Good Hope, and this 10 per cent special tea tax was charged on all tea exported by the way of Canada to the United

The Budget-Mr. Alesservy
States. Sir Francis Hincks immediately passed an act in the same session imposing a duty of 10 per cent on all tea coming from the United States. This act preserved to Canada its own tea trade and we enjoyed all its advantages. I understand that at the time the duty was fixed on eggs at three cents per dozen, the average price of eggs was fifteen cents per dozen which tax was figured at twenty per cent. But now that the price of eggs is forty cents per dozen, twenty per cent duty would be eight cents per dozen, which would be the same as the United States is charging us.
The West India treaty will be a good one for Canada and it should be given a fair trial. I have visited most of these islands several times and I know some of their requirements. The Maritime provinces should benefit by this treaty, especially Prince Edward Island, as many of our farm products and fish are wanted there. I want to impress upon the government the great necessity of having a steamer with cold storage accommodation call at Charlottetown going and coming from Montreal. There is a good market here for molasses from the West Indies, and we can give this steamer all kinds of produce: oats, potatoes, eggs, butter, cheese, cattle, horses and fish for the West Indies and Cuban market. Without the calling of this direct steamer the markets will be of very little use to us because railway freights are so high to Halifax, St. John and Montreal.
We all know that raw material is practically the advertisement for our vast Dominion to immigrants from abroad. An immense supply of timber, pulpwood, nickel, asbestos, minerals and such like draws the people here. We do not want our raw material to be shipped out of this Dominion, we want it here, and manufactured here. We want to feed the workers in the factories from the farms. Our raw material , is a guarantee for our debt and bonds which we have afloat and so on no account should it be allowed to leave this country. It may take a little time for us to give sufficient notice to people who have been trading in raw material with the United States, but the only true way to save Canada and help to pay off her debt is to prohibit the export of our raw material and manufacture it here. Let United States people who wish to make use of our raw materials in manufacturing come over here, and employ our Canadiain workmen in their factories in Canada instead of manufacturing our raw material in the United States.
I remember in 1897 being in Great Britain, and to show hon. members how anxious the Canadian Pacific railway was in soliciting im-
14011-1&&J
migrants for Canada, I was met in Bristol, London and Liverpool and presented with advertising matter regarding Canada: "One of the greatest countries in the world; all it needed was men. Are you going there?" I told them I was living in Canada. I remember I was canvassed publicly in that way on the streets. We should be determined at all times to have our agents in Great Britain, France, Norway. Sweden, Holland and Denmark do this persistent kind of canvassing. We will never succeed unless we push it quickly and firmly; quick action is necessary. Certainly our own Canadian people are the best, and every effort should be made to keep them at home because they are educated to our conditions; next to them come immigrants from the British Isles and France, then the Danes, Hollanders, Swedes and Norwegians. We rely upon the fairness and justice of our immigration agent in Great Britain to send us our fair share of immigrants, farmers, fishermen and capitalists, suitable to Prince Edward Island.
With regard to protection as an aid to Canadian farmers, I will quote in part what President Coolidge says about protection as an aid to the United States farmers:
Protection is a great benefit to agriculture as a whole. The $780,000,000 of agricultural produce imported lost year had to pay $260,000,000 for the privilege of coming in to compete with our own farm production. Protection greatly aids diversification and so eliminates an unprofitable surplus. Any study of dairy products, flax, wool and many other commodities will demonstrate that it does.
In aiding industry the present tariff helps agriculture because prosperity in our industries is of more value to the farmer than the whole export market for food stuffs.	,
I strongly support the policy of protection for farmers, manufacturers, merchants and fishermen. This was the clear-cut policy inaugurated in 187S by Sir John A. Macdonald, and the principle remains the same If we wish this great Canada of ours to be powerful and to get the large population she should have, we must adhere strictly to the policy of protection. Protection will bring immigrants to our shores and it will increase labour and instil confidence in our manufacturers.
We have many returned soldiers in Prince Edward Island and I wish now to speak for these as well as for the veterans in all parts of Canada. I ask hon. gentlemen to remember that while these men, our fellow Canadians, were suffering, bleeding, dying in the muddy fields of France and Flanders, the rest of us at home here were turning over inflated dividends or making big wages in war work, and every now and then we read of some veteran, too proud to beg and unable to

The Budget-Mr. Messervy
get work, who has decided to end it all by putting a bullet through his head! A charming spectacle this, is it not? We will not employ battle-scarred veterans because they are lazy and dissolute; our Board of Pension Commissioners sees to it that no man gets more than can be helped. What a praiseworthy example of economy in the public service! What, think you, would be your annual tribute to Germany to-day if these men had not won the war for us? A little more, I venture to say, than those pensions meted out with the greatest precaution taken to see that every hero gets not a cent more than is coming to him.
Such practice in dealing with our returned soldiers should come to an end; in fact it never should have existed at all. If a man has been taken on the strength of a unit and served overseas, and it is found on discharge that through illness or incapacity his earning power is diminished, he should be in receipt of a pension. Furthermore, it is up to every employer to give returned men the preference every time and, if necessary, legislation should be put into effect to make sure that every returned veteran has employment suited to his ability.
As for the "shiftlessness" and "drunkenness" of some of these men who have fought and bled for us there are few indeed who have come through four years of hell without scars of the spirit as well as of the body. I demand then, Sir, in the name of those who have fought and bled, in the name of those who have fallen, and in the name of the honour and decency of this Dominion, that no returned soldier, his wife or his family shall ever hereafter be allowed on any pretext whatever to want for food, clothes or home, or any of the common necessities or decencies of life.
In concluding, then, I wish first to appeal to our horn, friends from the great west sitting on this side of the House with us. Their honesty and integrity are unquestioned by all, and I am sure that all their actions here are guided by the larger interest of Canada, as they see it. To these hon. gentlemen I would submit that we do not come from Prince Edward Island, the little sister of the Dominion, and from the other provinces by the sea, as beggars imploring favours, but as equals asking for our rights. I am sure the hon. gentlemen from the other provinces see that we in the Maritimes could, from the nature of the case, have no share in the apportionment of the crown lands and territories. These Sir, rich as they are in farm lands, lumber, pulpwood and minerals, are

part of our heritage as well as theirs. Can they then grudge us the help we so sorely need? I feel sure they will not. And I appeal secondly to the hon. gentlemen opposite me, especially to our friends from Quebec. They have always stood out solidly for a vigorous Canadian nationalism. They know, Sir, that hurt to one of its members is an injury to the whole body. I am sure they would not wish to see the whole fabric of our country damaged by the neglect and starvation of its Maritime members. We depend upon the support and help of hon. members of the House of Commons.
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for your kind, courteous and considerate attention.
On motion of Mr. Marcil the debate was adjourned.
